bio.en: Nick Turley is the product lead for ChatGPT at OpenAI, having joined from Dropbox and Instacart, and helped turn a research project into the most consequential product in history.
bio.zh: 尼克·特利（Nick Turley）是 OpenAI 旗下 ChatGPT 的产品负责人，此前来自 Dropbox 和 Instacart，他帮助把一个研究项目变成了史上最具影响力的产品。

summary.en: Nick recalls joining OpenAI when it was a research lab and his first task was almost trivial, before helping build what became ChatGPT from a hackathon codebase. He shares the scrappy origin of a product initially expected to fail. The episode offers a behind-the-scenes look at shipping and scaling ChatGPT.
summary.zh: 尼克回忆，自己加入 OpenAI 时它还只是研究实验室，第一个任务近乎琐碎，之后才参与把一个黑客松代码库做成了 ChatGPT。他分享了这款最初被认为会失败的产品——ChatGPT——的草创起源。本期提供了 ChatGPT 上线与规模化的幕后视角。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You were a product leader at Dropbox, then Instacart. Now, you're the PM of the most consequential product in history.
turns.zh: 你曾先后担任Dropbox和Instacart的产品负责人，如今又执掌着史上最具影响力的产品——Facebook Messenger。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I didn't know what I would do here because it was a research lab. My first task was I fix the blinds, or something like that.
turns.zh: 我不知道自己在这儿该做些什么，毕竟这是一间研究实验室。我的首项任务是修理百叶窗之类的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When someone offers you a rocket ship, don't ask which seat.
turns.zh: 当有人给你提供一艘火箭飞船时，别去纠结该选哪个座位。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: We set out to build a super assistant. It was supposed to be a hackathon code base.
turns.zh: 我们着手打造一个超级助手。这原本应该是一个黑客马拉松项目的代码库。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was it called before?
turns.zh: 它之前叫什么名字？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It was going to be Chat with GPT-3.5 because we really didn't think it was going to be a successful product.
turns.zh: 原本打算用GPT-3.5进行聊天功能测试，因为我们当时实在不认为这款产品能取得成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then Sam Altman is just like, "Hey, let me tweet about it."
turns.zh: 然后萨姆·奥尔特曼就随口说了一句：“嘿，我来发条推特说说这事吧。”

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: This is a pattern with AI, you won't know what to polish until after you ship. My dream is that we ship daily.
turns.zh: 这是人工智能带来的一个模式——在产品上线之前，你根本不知道该优化哪些地方。我的理想状态是我们能做到每日上线新功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the time people hear this, they're going to have their hands on GPT-5.
turns.zh: 等人们听说这件事的时候，GPT-5很可能已经正式发布了。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: About 10% of the world population uses every week. With scale comes responsibility. It just feels a little bit more alive, a bit more human. This model has taste.
turns.zh: 全球约有10%的人口每周都会使用这款产品。规模越大，责任越重。它总能让人感觉更具生机，更富有人性。这款产品的设计理念堪称精妙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kevin Weil, your CPO, said to ask you about this principle of, "Is it maximally accelerated?"
turns.zh: 你的首席产品官凯文·韦尔让我问你一个原则：“它是否实现了最大程度的加速？”

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I just really want to jump to the punchline, "Why can't we do this now?" I always felt like part of my role here is to just set the pace and the resting heartbeat.
turns.zh: 我真的很想直接说出关键问题：“为什么我们现在就不能行动呢？” 我总觉得，在这里我的职责之一就是设定节奏，保持团队的稳定运作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone is always wondering, "Is Chat the future of all of this stuff?"
turns.zh: 大家总是会好奇：“聊天功能会是所有这些应用的未来吗？”

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Chat was the simplest way to ship at that time. I'm baffled by how much it took off, even more baffled by how many people have copied.
turns.zh: 当时用聊天工具发货是最简单的方式了。我真不明白它怎么能火成这样，更不明白为什么有那么多人模仿它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ChatGPT is now driving more traffic to my newsletter than Twitter.
turns.zh: 如今，ChatGPT为我的新闻通讯带来的流量比推特还要多。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: That is the type of capability that has been incredibly retentive. I've been really excited about what we've been doing in search.
turns.zh: 这种能力实在是令人惊叹。我对我们在搜索领域所做的工作一直倍感振奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you give us a peek into where this goes long-term?
turns.zh: 能否给我们透露一下这项工作的长期发展方向？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: ChatGPT feels a little bit like MS-DOS. We haven't built Windows yet, and it will be obvious once we do.
turns.zh: 聊天机器人ChatGPT给人的感觉有点像MS-DOS系统。我们目前还没有开发出Windows操作系统，但等我们真正开发出来后，其差异就会一目了然了。

turns.zh: 我本来就有一亿个问题想问你，结果你们偏偏在我们录制这期节目的那周推出了GPT-5。现在我至少有二十亿个问题要问你们了。希望你们有充足的时间。首先，恭喜你们成功上线！新版本明天就会发布，也就是录制完这期节目后的第二天。真心祝贺！你现在感觉怎么样？我能想象这项工作量巨大、压力十足。你们目前进展如何？

turns.zh: 这周很忙，但我们为此已经努力了一段时间，所以现在终于能把成果呈现出来，感觉真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, by the time people hear this, they're going to have their hands on GPT-5, the newest ChatGPT. What's the simplest way to just understand what this is, what it unlocks, what people can do with it? Give us the pitch.
turns.zh: 等大家听完这段介绍的时候，他们手里应该已经拿到了GPT-5，也就是最新版的ChatGPT。那么，要怎样才能最简单地理解这项技术、它能带来哪些突破、人们又能用它做些什么呢？请给我们来个快速介绍吧。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I'm so excited about GPT-5. I think for most people, it's going to feel like a real step change. If you're the average ChatGPT user, and we have 700 million of them this week, you've probably been on GPT-4o for a while. You probably don't even think about the model that powers the product. And GPT-5, it just feels categorically different. I'll talk about a lot of the specifics, but at the end of the day, the vibes are good, at least we feel that way. We hope that users feel the same. And increasingly, that is the thing that I think most people notice, right? They don't look at the academic benchmarks. They don't look at evaluations. They try the model and see what it feels like. And just on that dimension alone, I'm so excited. I've been using it for a while, but it is also the smartest, most useful, and fastest frontier model that we've ever launched. (00:06:33): On pure SMARTs, one way to look at that is academic benchmarks on many of the standard ones, whether or not it's math, or reasoning, or just raw intelligence. This model is state of the art. I'm especially excited about its performance on coding, whether or not that's SWE-bench, which is a common benchmark, or actually front-end coding is really, really good as well, and that's an area where I feel like there's the true step change improvement in GPT-5. But really, no matter how you measure the SMARTs, it's quite remarkable, and I think people are going to feel the upgrade, especially if they weren't using o3 already. (00:07:13): And the second thing beyond SMARTs is it's just really useful. Coding is one axis of utility, whether or not you have coding questions or you're vibe coding an app, but it's also a really good writer. I write for a living, internally, externally. I just wrote a big blog post that we published Monday, and this thing is such an incredible editor. And compared to some of the older models, it's got taste, which I think is really exciting. And to me, that's something that is truly useful in my day-to-day. And there's a bunch of other areas, like it's state of the art on health, which is useful when you need it, but again, the thing you can't really express in use cases or data is the vibe of the model. And it just feels a little bit more alive, a bit more human in a way that is hard to articulate until you try it. So, feel good about that. (00:08:06): And yeah, as mentioned, it's faster. It thinks, too, just like o3 did, but you don't have to manually tell it to do that. It'll just dynamically decide to think when it needs to. And when it doesn't need to think, it just responds instantly, and that ends up feeling quite a bit faster than using o3 did. And then maybe the thing that's most exciting is that we're making it available for free, and that's one of those things that I feel like we can uniquely do at OpenAI. Because many companies, I think, if they have a subscription model like us, they would gate it behind their paid plan. And for us, if we can scale it, we will, and that just feels awesome. We did that with 4o as well. So, everyone is going to be able to try GPT-5 tomorrow, hopefully.
turns.zh: 我对GPT-5感到无比兴奋。我认为对大多数人来说，这将是一次真正的技术革命。如果你是ChatGPT的普通用户——本周我们已有7亿用户——你可能已经用了GPT-4o一段时间了。你甚至可能从未想过支撑这款产品的模型到底是什么。而GPT-5给人的感觉截然不同。我会详细讲解其技术细节，但归根结底，整体体验非常棒，至少我们自己是这么认为的。希望用户也能感受到这一点。而越来越多的人注意到的正是这一点，对吧？他们不会去关注学术基准测试，也不会去评判模型表现。他们会亲自试用，感受其使用体验。仅从这一维度来看，我就无比激动。尽管我已经使用了一段时间，但GPT-5仍是我们推出的最智能、最实用、速度最快的前沿模型。（00:06:33）：在纯粹的智能指标（SMARTs）方面，我们可以从多个标准基准来衡量，比如数学、推理或纯粹的智力水平。这款模型达到了业界顶尖水平。我对其在编程领域的表现尤为兴奋，无论是SWE基准测试（常见的编程测试标准），还是前端编码都表现出色。这正是GPT-5真正实现技术飞跃的领域。但无论如何衡量智能指标，它的表现都令人惊叹，我相信用户会感受到这种升级，特别是如果他们之前没有使用o3的话。（00:07:13）：除了智能指标，GPT-5还非常实用。在实用性方面

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long does something like this take? I don't know if there's a simple answer to this, but just how long have you guys been working on GPT-5?
turns.zh: 像这样的事情需要多长时间？我不知道有没有一个简单的答案，但你们研发GPT-5到底花了多长时间？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: We've been working on it for a while. You can view GPT-5 as a culmination of a bunch of different efforts. We had a reasoning tech, we had a more classic post-screening methodologies, and therefore, it's really hard to put a beginning on it, but it really is the end point of a bunch of different techniques that we began for a while.
turns.zh: 我们已经研究这个项目有一段时间了。你可以把GPT-5看作是诸多不同研究方向的集大成者。我们研发了推理技术，也探索了更为传统的后筛选方法。因此，要确定它的起点其实很难，但它确实是我们多年来积累的各种技术的最终成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you give us a peek into the vision for where ChatGPT is going, GPT in general is going? If you look at on the surface, it's been the same idea with a much smarter brain for a long time. I'm curious where this goes long-term.
turns.zh: 能否请您为我们解读一下ChatGPT的发展方向，以及GPT技术整体的发展愿景？从表面上看，多年来GPT的核心理念始终如一——只不过现在其"大脑"变得更加智能了。我很好奇这种技术在未来会有怎样的长远发展前景。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: So, to maybe back up a bit, now, you think of ChatGPT as, "Is this going to be ubiquitous product?" Again, about 10% of the world population uses every week.
turns.zh: So, to maybe back up a bit, now, you think of ChatGPT as, "Is this going to be ubiquitous product?" Again, about 10% of the world population uses every week.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy shit.
turns.zh: 天啊！

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I think we have 5 million business customers now. It's an established category in its own right. But really, when we started, we set out to build a super assistant, that's how we talked about it at the time. In fact, the code base that we use is called SA Server. It was supposed to be a hackathon code base, but things always turn out a little bit differently. So, yeah, in some ways, that is still the vision. The reason I don't talk about it more than I do is because I think assistant is a bit limiting in terms of the mental model we're trying to create. You think of this very personified human thing, maybe utilitarian, maybe a... And frankly, having an assistant is not particularly relatable to most people, unless they're in Silicon Valley and they're a manager, or something like that. So it's imperfect. (00:10:24): But really, what we envision is this entity that can help you with any task, whether or not that's at home, or at work, or at school, really any context, and it's an entity that knows what you're trying to achieve. So, unlike ChatGPT today, you don't have to describe your problem in menu to detail because it already stands your overarching goals and has context on your life, et cetera. So, that's one thing that we're really excited about. The inverse of giving it more inputs on your life is giving it more action space. So, we're really excited to allow it to do, over time, what a smart, empathetic human with a computer could do for you. And I think the limit of the types of problems that you can solve for people, once you give it access to tools like that, is very, very different than what you might be able to do in a chatbot today. So, that's more outputs. (00:11:19): And I often think, "Okay, I'm a general intelligence. What happened if I became Lenny's intern, or something?" And I wouldn't be particularly effective despite having both of those attributes that I just mentioned, and it's because I think this idea of building a relationship with this technology is also incredibly important. So, that's maybe the third piece that I'm excited about is building a product that can truly get to know you over time. And you saw us launch some of those things with improved memory earlier this year, and that's just the beginning of what we're hoping to do so that it really feels like this is your AI. So, I don't know if supersystem is still the right exact analogy, but I think people just think of it as their AI. And I think we can put one in everyone's pocket and help them solve real problems, whether or not that's becoming healthy, whether or not that's starting a business, whether or not that's just having a second opinion on anything. There's so many different problems that you can help with people in their daily life, and that's what motivates me.
turns.zh: 我认为我们现在有500万商业客户。这本身已经是一个成熟的品类。但说真的，我们刚起步时，就立志打造一个超级助手——当时我们就是这么说的。事实上，我们使用的代码库叫SA Server。它本该是一个黑客马拉松项目的代码库，但事情总会有些出乎意料。所以，是的，在某种程度上，这依然是我们的愿景。我之所以不常提及它，是因为我认为助手这个概念在我们试图构建的心智模型中存在局限性。人们往往会联想到一个极具人格化的存在，或许实用性强，或许……说实话，助手概念对大多数人来说并不亲切，除非他们身处硅谷，是个经理之类的人物。所以它并不完美。（00:10:24）但实际上，我们的愿景是创造一个能在任何场景——无论是家庭、工作还是学校——帮助你完成任务的实体。它要能理解你的目标。所以与当今的ChatGPT不同，你无需逐条描述问题，因为它已经掌握了你的总体目标，了解你的生活背景等信息。这正是我们最兴奋的点之一。赋予它更多生活数据的反面，是赋予它更大的行动空间。因此，我们迫切希望它能逐渐做到像一个聪明、善解人意的人类助手一样为你服务。我认为，一旦赋予它类似工具的访问权限，人们可解决的问题类型将远超当今聊天机器人所能处理的范畴。这就是更深层的输出层面。（00:11:19）我常想：“好吧，我是个通用智能系统。如果我成了莱尼的实习生之类的，会怎样？”即便拥有上述两个特质，我也未必能高效工作，因为我认为与这项技术建立情感联结同样重要。这或许是我最期待的第三个核心要素——打造一款能随着时间推移真正了解你的产品。今年早些时候，我们推出了记忆力增强功能，这只是冰山一角。我们的目标是让它真正成为你的AI助手。我不确定“超级系统”是否仍是贴切的比喻，但人们确实把它视为自己的AI。我们希望能让每个人口袋里都装着这样一个助手，无论是助力健康管理、创业，还是获取第二意见。它能解决人们日常生活中的诸多难题，这就是我的动力所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So an interesting between the lines that I'm reading here is the vision is for it to be an assistant for people not to replace people. It feels like a really important piece of the puzzle. Maybe just talk about that.
turns.zh: 嗯，我在这里读到的潜在信息很有意思，他们的愿景是让这款产品成为人类的助手，而不是取代人类。这感觉像是整个拼图中至关重要的一块。或许你可以再详细谈谈这一点。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: AI is really scary to people, and I understand there's decades of movies on AI that have a certain mental model baked in. And even if you just look at the technology today, everyone, I think, has this moment where the AI does something that was really deeply personal to them and you're thought, "Hey, AI can never do that." For me, it was weird music theory things where I was like, "Wow, this thing actually understands music better than I do," and that's something I'm passionate about. And so it's naturally scary. And I think the thing that's been really important to us for a long time is to build something that feels like it's helpful to you, but you're in the driver's seat, and that's even more important as the stuff becomes agentic, the feeling of being in control, and that can be small things. (00:13:15): We built this way of watching what the AI is doing when it's in agent mode. And it's not that you actually are going to watch it the whole time, but it gives you a mental model and makes you feel in control in the same way that, when you're in a Waymo, you get that screen, for those of you who've tried Waymo. You can see the other cars. It's not like you're going to actually watch, but it gives you the sense that you know how this thing works and what's happening, or we always check with you to confirm things. It's a little bit annoying, but it puts you in the driver's seat, which is important. And for that reason, we always view technology and the technology that we build as something that amplifies what you're capable of, rather than replacing it, and that becomes important as the deck gets more powerful.
turns.zh:
人工智能确实让人们感到恐惧。我理解，几十年来关于人工智能的电影都深深植入了某种思维模式。即便以当今的技术水平来看，我相信每个人都曾经历过这样的时刻：人工智能做出了某件与自己息息相关的事情，你会感叹"天啊，人工智能永远做不到这件事"。对我而言，这样的时刻是一些奇特的音乐理论知识——比如"哇，这东西对音乐的理解比我还要深刻"，而音乐恰恰是我所热爱的。所以这种不安感很自然地产生了。长期以来，对我们而言至关重要的是，要打造出既能提供帮助又让用户掌控全局的产品。随着技术的不断进化，掌控感愈发重要，哪怕是一些细微的举动也能体现这一点。

（00:13:15）我们开发了这样一种方式：当人工智能处于自主模式时，用户可以实时观察其行为。当然，你不会一直盯着屏幕看，但这种视觉反馈能让用户建立心理模型，获得掌控感。就好比乘坐Waymo自动驾驶汽车时，你会看到屏幕上的其他车辆。虽然你不会全程监控，但这种可视化能让你清楚车辆的运行机制，或是通过交互式确认当前状态。这听起来有点烦人，但它能让用户感受到自己对技术的掌控感，这一点至关重要。因此，我们始终将技术视为增强人类能力的工具，而非替代品。随着技术实力不断提升，这种设计理念将变得更加重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you mentioned the beginnings of ChatGPT. I was reading in a different interview. So you joined OpenAI. ChatGPT was just this internal experimental project that was basically a way to test GPT-3.5, and then Sam Altman is just like, "Hey, let me tweet about it, maybe see if people find this interesting," yada yada, yada. It's the most successful consumer product in history, I think both in growth rate in users and revenue, and just absurd. Can you give us a glimpse into that early period before it became something everyone is obsessed with?
turns.zh: 好的。你之前提到了ChatGPT的起源。我在另一篇采访中看到过相关内容。当时你加入了OpenAI，ChatGPT最初只是一个内部实验项目，旨在测试GPT-3.5的性能。然后Sam Altman就发推文宣传了一下，看看大家是否感兴趣之类的。结果它成了史上最成功的消费级产品，无论是用户增长率还是营收表现都堪称惊人。你能给我们讲讲它从实验项目到引发全民热潮的早期历程吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. So we had decided that we wanted to do something consumer-facing, I think, right around the time that GPT-4 finished training, and it was actually mainly for a couple of reasons. We already had a product out there, which was our developer product. That's actually what I came in to help with initially, and that has been amazing for the mission. In fact, it's grown up. And now, it's the OpenAI platform with, I don't know, 4 million developers, I think. But at that time, it was early stage, and we were running into some constraints with it because there was two problems. One, you couldn't iterate very quickly because, every time you would change the model, you'd break everyone's app. So, it was really hard to try things. (00:15:03): And then the other thing was that it was really hard to learn because the feedback we would get was the feedback from the end user to the developer to us. So it was very disintermediated, and we were excited to make fast progress towards AGI and it just felt like we needed a more direct relationship with consumers. So we were trying to figure out where to start. And in classic OpenAI fashion, especially back then, we put together a hackathon of enthusiasts of just hacking on GPT-4 to see what awesome stuff we could create and maybe ship to users, and everyone's idea was some flavor of a super assistant. They were more specific ideas, like we had a meeting bot that would call into meetings, and the vision was maybe it would help you run the meeting over time. We had a coding tool, which full circle now, probably ahead of its time. And the challenge was that we tested those things, but every time we tested these more bespoke ideas, people wanted to use it for all this other stuff because it's just a very, very generically powerful technology. (00:16:04): So, after a couple of months of prototyping, we took that same crew of volunteers, and it was truly a volunteer group, right? We had someone from the supercomputing team who had built an iOS app before. We had someone on the research team who had written some backend code in their life. They were all part of this initial ChatGPT team, and we decided to ship something open-ended because we just wanted a real use case distribution. And this is a pattern with AI, I think, where you really have to ship to understand what is even possible and what people want, rather than being able to reason about that a priori. So, ChatGPT came together at the end because we just wanted the learnings as soon as we could, and we shipped it right before the holiday thinking we would come back and get the data and then wind it down. And obviously, that part turned out super differently because people really liked the product as is. (00:16:56): So I remember going through the motions of like, "Oh, man, dashboard is broken. Oh, wait, people are liking it. I'm sure it's just going viral and stuff is going to die down," to like, "Oh, wow, people are retaining, but I don't understand why." And then eventually, we fell into product development mode, but it was a little bit by accident.
turns.zh:
是的。所以我们决定要做面向消费者的产品，我想这是在GPT-4完成训练后不久的决定，主要有几个原因。当时我们已经推出了面向开发者的产品，这实际上是我最初加入OpenAI帮助开发的产品，它对我们的使命非常有帮助。事实上，它后来发展得很好。我记得现在OpenAI平台上有大约400万开发者。但当时它还处于早期阶段，我们遇到了两个问题：一是模型每次更新都会导致所有应用崩溃，所以迭代速度很慢；二是反馈链路太长——用户的反馈要经过开发者才能传达给我们，缺乏直接沟通。当时我们迫切希望在通用人工智能（AGI）方面取得进展，觉得需要与消费者建立更直接的联系，于是决定尝试从零开始。

以OpenAI一贯的作风，特别是当时的团队，我们举办了一场黑客马拉松，让对GPT-4感兴趣的志愿者们自由探索，看看能创造出什么惊喜成果。大家提出的都是超级助手类型的想法，比如会主动加入会议的会议机器人，还有帮助远程管理会议的工具。当时我们还开发了一个编码工具，现在看来这个功能确实超前了。但问题是，每次测试这些定制化方案时，用户总想把它用于其他场景，因为GPT-4实在是太通用、太强大了。

经过几个月的原型开发，我们召集了同样一批志愿者（当时确实是个志愿者团队），成员包括曾开发过iOS应用的超级计算团队成员，以及有后端开发经验的研究团队成员。他们组成了最初的ChatGPT团队。我们决定推出开放式产品，专注于真实的使用场景分布。我认为这正是AI领域的典型模式——你必须先推向市场，才能真正理解用户需求和技术潜力，而非凭空推测。最终ChatGPT得以问世，因为我们迫切想尽快获得反馈，并计划在假期前下线服务。但结果出乎意料——用户对现有产品爱不释手。

记得当时我不断自我怀疑：仪表板崩溃了？用户却很喜欢？数据滞留了？但最终我们不由自主地进入了产品开发模式，虽然过程有些曲折。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I did not know that ChatGPT emerged out of a hackathon project. Definitely the most successful hackathon project.
turns.zh: 哇哦。我之前都不知道ChatGPT是从一个黑客马拉松项目中诞生的。这绝对是最成功的黑客马拉松项目了。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I like to tell this story when we do our hackathons because I really do want people to feel like they can ship their idea, and it's certainly been true in the past, and we'll continue to make it true.
turns.zh: 在我们举办黑客马拉松活动时，我总喜欢讲这个故事，因为我真心希望人们能感受到，他们完全有能力将自己的创意变为现实。过去确实如此，未来我们也会继续努力让这一愿景成为现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you don't want to share these things, but I wonder who that team was.
turns.zh: 如果你不想分享这些信息的话，不过我很好奇那个团队是谁啊。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: The team is largely still around. Some of the researchers working on GPT-5, actually, were always part of the ChatGPT team. Engineers are still around. Designers are still around. I'm still here, I guess. So, yeah, you've got the team still running things, but obviously, we've grown up tremendously, and we've had to because with scale comes responsibility. And we're going to hit a billion users soon and you have to begin acting in a way that is appropriate to that scale.
turns.zh: 团队的大部分成员依然在岗。实际上，参与GPT-5研发的一些研究人员，从一开始就是ChatGPT团队的成员。工程师们还在，设计师们也还在。我想我也还在。所以，是的，团队依然在运作，但显然我们已经有了长足的发展——毕竟规模越大，责任越重。我们很快就要迎来十亿用户了，这就要求我们必须以与之相匹配的规模来行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So let me spend a little time there. So, I don't know if this is 100% true, but I believe it is that ChatGPT is the fastest growing, most successful consumer product in history. Also, the most impactful on people's lives. It feels like it's just part of the ether of society now. It's just my wife talks to it. Every question I have, I go to it, voice mode. My wife is just like, "Let me check with ChatGPT." It's just such a part of our life now, and I think it's still early. So many people don't even know what the hell is going on. Just as someone leading this, do you ever just take a moment to reflect and think about just like, "Holy shit"?
turns.zh: 好的。那让我先稍微讲一下。我不知道这是否百分之百准确，但我认为ChatGPT是史上增长最快、最成功的消费级产品。它对人们生活的影响也极为深远。如今它仿佛已融入社会的方方面面。我妻子经常和它对话。我每次有问题都会用语音模式询问ChatGPT。她总是说"让我问问ChatGPT吧"。它现在已经成了我们生活不可或缺的一部分，而我觉得这才刚刚起步。太多人甚至不明白到底怎么回事。作为负责这项技术的人，你有没有过片刻停下来，感叹一句"天哪"？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I have to. It's quite humbling to get to run a product like that, and I have to pinch myself very frequently, and I also have to sometimes sit back and just think, which is really hard when things are moving so quickly. I love setting a fast pace at the company, but in order to do that with confidence, I need at least one day every week that I'm entirely unplugged and I'm just thinking about what to do and process the week, et cetera. (00:19:14): And the other thing is I've never ever worked on a product that is so empirical in its nature where, if you don't stop, and watch, and listen to what people are doing, you're going to miss so much, both on the utility and on the risks, actually. Because normally, by the time you ship a product, you know what it's going to do. You don't know if people are going to like it, that's always empirical, but you know what it can do. And with AI, because I think so much of it is emergent, you actually really need to stop and listen after you launch something and then iterate on the things people are trying to do and on the things that aren't quite working yet. So, for that reason alone, I think it's very important to take a break and just watch what's going on.
turns.zh:
我必须这样做。能负责运营这样一款产品，确实让我倍感荣幸。我常常得掐自己一下，有时还得静下心来思考——尤其是在事情进展太快的时候，这真的很不容易。我喜欢在公司保持快节奏，但要想从容做到这一点，每周至少得有一天完全放空大脑，思考下周的计划，整理思绪等。

（00:19:14）还有一点，我从未参与过如此强调实证性的产品研发项目。如果你不去观察、倾听用户行为，就很可能错过关键信息——无论是产品功能的实用性，还是潜在风险的识别。通常在产品上线时，开发者已经预判了其功能效果。虽然用户喜好仍是未知数，但至少功能本身是确定的。而人工智能领域的情况则完全不同，因为其核心逻辑具有高度涌现性。在产品上线后，你必须停下脚步倾听用户反馈，迭代那些尚未完善的功能或用户尝试但未达成预期的地方。正因如此，我认为定期停下来观察产品运行情况至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you take a day off every week... not off. Okay, that's not the right way to put it. You take a day of thinking time, deep work.
turns.zh: 好的。所以你每周会专门留出一天时间……不，是专门留出一天用于思考、深度工作的时段。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I need it. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And I need to hard unplug on a Saturday, or something like that. Obviously-
turns.zh: 我需要它。是啊，是啊，是啊。我得在周六彻底放松一下，或者做点类似的事。显然——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On a Saturday [inaudible 00:20:16].

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: But it's just not possible otherwise. This has been a giant marathon for three years now. Yeah.
turns.zh: 但除此之外别无他法。这场马拉松式的战斗已经持续了整整三年。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like a sprint marathon.
turns.zh: 就像一场短跑马拉松。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Sprint marathon, that's right, or interval training, or something. I don't know how to exactly describe the OpenAI launch cadence, but you've got to set yourself up in a way that is sustainable. Even if this wasn't AI and it didn't have the interesting attributes that I just mentioned, I think you would need to do that. But especially with AI, it's important to go watch.
turns.zh: 短跑马拉松，对，没错，或者是间歇训练之类的。我不知道该如何准确描述OpenAI的发布节奏，但你必须要确保自己的节奏是可持续的。即便这不是人工智能领域，也没有我刚才提到的那些有趣特性，我觉得你也得这么做。但对于人工智能领域而言，持续关注其发展动态尤为重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, along those lines, I talked to a bunch of people that work with you, that work at OpenAI. Joanne specifically said that urgency and pace are a big part of how you operate, that that's just something you find really important, to create urgency within the team constantly, even when you are the fastest growing product in history, growing like crazy. Talk about just your philosophy on the importance of pace and urgency on teams.
turns.zh: 基于此，我和许多在OpenAI工作的同事进行了交流。乔安妮特别指出，紧迫感和快节奏是你们团队运作的重要因素——你们始终将营造团队的紧迫感视为重中之重，即便在你们的产品以史无前例的速度疯狂增长时，也要持续激发团队的紧迫感。请谈谈您对团队中速度与紧迫感重要性的看法。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Well, it's nice of her to say that. Two things, with ChatGPT, when we decided to do it, we had been prototyping for so long and I was just like, "In 10 days, we're going to ship this thing," and we did. So, that was maybe a moment in time thing where I just really wanted to make sure that we go learn something. Ever since then, I spent so much time thinking about why ChatGPT became successful in the first place, and I think there was some element of just doing things where there was many other companies that had technology in the LLM space that just never got shipped. And I just felt like, of all the things we could optimize for, learning as fast as possible is incredibly important. So I just started rallying people around that, and that took different forms. (00:21:55): For a while, when we were of that size, I just ran this daily release sync and had everyone who was required to make a decision in it, and we would just talk about what to do and to pivot from yesterday, et cetera. Obviously, at some point, that doesn't scale, but I always felt like part of my role here, obviously, was to think about the direction of the product, but also to just set the pace and the resting heartbeat for our teams. And again, this is important anywhere, but it's especially important when the only way to find out what people like and what's valuable is to bring it into the external world. So, for that reason, I think it's become a superpower of OpenAI, and I'm glad that Joanne thinks that I had some part in that, but it really has taken a village.
turns.zh: 嗯，她这么说真是太好了。关于ChatGPT，有两件事值得一提。当时我们决定启动这个项目时，已经原型开发了很久，而我当时就说"十天内我们要把这东西推向市场"，然后我们做到了。所以，那可能是一个特定时刻——我当时特别想确保团队能从中吸取经验。自那以后，我花了大量时间思考ChatGPT成功的根本原因。我认为，其中一个关键点在于，许多其他公司在LLM领域拥有技术却始终未能成功推向市场。而我深信，在所有可以优化的方面，尽快学习新事物至关重要。因此，我开始围绕这一理念团结团队，具体形式多种多样。（00:21:55）在公司规模较小时，我们每日举行发布协调会，让所有需要参与决策的人参与其中，共同探讨当天的工作重点和调整方向。显然，这种模式最终无法扩展，但我始终认为，我的职责不仅在于规划产品方向，更要为团队设定节奏和基准。无论在何种环境下，这一点都至关重要，但当产品价值的唯一验证途径是推向外部市场时，这一点就显得尤为重要。因此，我认为这已成为OpenAI的核心竞争力之一。我很欣慰乔安妮认为我对此有所贡献，但这确实是团队共同努力的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this phrase, "the resting heart rate of your team". That's such a perfect metaphor of just the pace of being equivalent to your resting heart rate.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这句话：“你团队的静息心率”。这简直是绝妙的比喻，将团队的运作节奏比作静息心率，真是太贴切了。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I actually learned that at Instacart, when I showed up there, because we were in the pandemic and it was all hands on deck. For a while, there was this... I think there was a company-wide stand-up because we disbanded all teams. We were just trying to keep the site up. And for me, I had been used to taking my sweet time and just thinking really hard about things, and that's important, but I really learned to hustle over there, and I think that's come in handy at OpenAI.
turns.zh: 事实上，我是在Instacart公司才意识到这一点的。当时正值疫情期间，全公司都需要全力以赴。有一阵子，公司组织了全员站会，因为当时所有团队都被解散了，大家只能齐心协力维持网站正常运转。说到我自己，我向来习惯从容不迫，深思熟虑地处理问题——这固然重要，但在Instacart的经历让我真正学会了如何高效行动。我认为这份能力在OpenAI也派上了大用场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, along these same lines, I asked Kevin Weil, your CPO, what to ask you, and he said to ask you about this principle of, "Is it maximally accelerated?" Talk about that.
turns.zh: 好的。那么，沿着同样的思路，我问了你们的首席产品官凯文·韦尔该问您什么问题，他说要问您关于“是否实现了最大加速度”这个原则。请您谈谈这个问题。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: That's funny, we have a Slack emoji, apparently, for this now because I used to say that. Now, I try to paraphrase. Sometimes, I just really want to jump to the punchline of like, "Okay, why can't we do this now?" or, "Why can't we do it tomorrow?" And I think that it's a good way to cut through a huge number of blockers with the team and just instill... especially if you come from a larger company. At some point, we started hiring people from larger tech companies. I think they're used to, "Let's check in on this in a week," or, "Let's circle back next quarter to see if we can go on the plan." And I just, as a-
turns.zh: 真有意思，我们Slack平台现在居然专门为这种情况设计了一个表情符号——显然是因为我以前老是这么说了。现在我尽量换个说法。有时候我特别想直接抛出关键问题，比如“好吧，为什么我们现在就不能做这个？”或者“为什么我们不能明天就开始？”我觉得这能有效突破团队中大量阻碍进展的障碍，尤其是在大型公司任职的情况下。我们公司从某个阶段开始，开始从大型科技公司招聘员工。我发现他们习惯说“我们一周后再评估”或者“下个季度再重新评估是否能按计划推进”。而我呢，总是——

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: ... on the plan and I just kind of as a thought exercise, always like people asking, "Okay, if this was the most important thing and you wanted to truly maximally accelerate it, what would you do?" That doesn't mean that you go do that, but it's really a good forcing function for understanding what's critical path versus what can happen later. And I've just always felt like execution is incredibly important. These ideas, they're everywhere. Everyone's talking about a personal AI, you might've seen news on that and I really think that execution is one of the most important things in the space and this is a tool. So, it's funny that that became a meme. It's like a little pink Slack emoji that people just put on whatever they're trying to force the question.
turns.zh: ……关于这个计划，我只是把它当作一种思维练习。总有人会问：“好吧，如果这是最重要的事，而你又想尽可能快地推进它，你会怎么做？”这并不意味着你真的要去那么做，但它确实能很好地促使你分清什么是关键路径，什么是可以稍后再处理的事务。我一直觉得执行力至关重要。这些理念无处不在。大家都在谈论个人AI，你可能也看到过相关新闻。我真的认为执行力是这个领域最重要的要素之一，而这就是一个工具。说来有趣，它后来还成了一个梗。就像那个粉色Slack表情符号，人们会把它贴在任何想强制思考这个问题的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to ask, what theme [inaudible 00:24:47]. So, it's a little pink, is there something in there like-
turns.zh: 我本来想问，主题是什么（00:24:47处语音不清）。嗯，整体是粉色调的，里面有没有什么特别的元素之类的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It's a Comic Sans emoji that says, is this maximally accelerated?
turns.zh: 这是一个用Comic Sans字体呈现的表情符号，配文写着："这是最大限度加速了吗？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And so, the kind of the culture there is when someone is working on something, the push is, is this maximally accelerated? Is there a way we can do this faster? Is there anything we can unblock?
turns.zh: 好的。那么，在那里的文化氛围中，当有人在做某件事时，大家会追问：这项工作能否最大限度地提速？有没有办法能让进度更快？有没有什么障碍需要突破？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. And we use that sparingly, right? Because it needs to be appropriate to the context. There's some things where you don't want to accelerate as quickly as possible because you kind of want process. And we're very, very deliberate on that where your process is a tool. And one of the areas where we have an immense amount of process is safety. Because A, the stakes are already really high, especially with these models, GPT-5 which is a frontier in so many different ways. But B, if you believe in the exponential, which I do and most people who work on this stuff do, you have to play practice for a time where you really, really need the process for sure, sure, sure. And that's why I think it's been really important to separate out the product development velocity, which has to be super high from, for things like frontier models, there actually needs to be a rigorous process where you red team, you work on the system card, you get external input, and then you put things out with confidence that it's gone through the right safeguards. (00:26:02): So, again, it's a nuanced concept, but I found it very, very useful when we needed and for everything product development, you're a dead on arrival, so it's important to get stuff out.
turns.zh: 是的。而且我们要谨慎使用这种方法，对吧？因为它必须符合上下文需求。有些情况下，你不宜急于求成，因为你需要一个循序渐进的过程。在这些领域，流程本身就是一种工具。比如安全领域，我们在这方面投入了极其繁琐的流程。首先，安全风险本就极高，尤其是像GPT-5这样在诸多方面都开创先河的模型。其次，如果你认同指数级增长的理念（我深信这一点，大多数从事这项研究的人也都认同），那么在你确实迫切需要流程的时候，比如在突破性模型开发阶段，严密的流程就显得至关重要。这就是为什么我认为区分产品开发速度和前沿模型开发速度非常重要。前者必须保持极高的效率；而后者则需要严格的流程——比如开展红队评估、撰写系统文档、收集外部反馈——只有这样，我们才能充满信心地将经过层层把关的成果推向市场。（00:26:02）所以说，这是一个需要细致权衡的概念。但当我们开发产品时，时间就是生命，尽快推出成果至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We got to open source those memes so that other teams can build on this approach.
turns.zh: 我们得把那些梗图开源，这样其他团队就能在此基础上进一步创新了。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错，完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, interestingly with ChatGPT, and it's not a surprise, but not only is it the fastest-growing, most successful consumer product ever, retention is also incredibly high. People have shared these stats that one month retention is something like 90%, six month retention is something like 80%. First of all, are these numbers accurate? What can you share there?
turns.zh: 嗯，有趣的是，就ChatGPT而言，这并不令人意外。它不仅是史上增长最快、最成功的消费级产品，而且用户留存率也极高。有人分享过相关数据，比如一个月的用户留存率约为90%，六个月的用户留存率约为80%。首先，这些数据是否准确呢？你能否再补充一些相关信息？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I'm obviously limited on what exactly I can share, but it is true that our retention numbers are really exciting and that is actually the thing we look at. We don't care at all how much time you spend in the product. In fact, our incentive is just to solve your problem and if you really like the product, you'll subscribe, but there's no incentive to keep you in the product for long. But we are obviously really, really happy if over the long run, three month period, et cetera, you're still using this thing. And for me, this was always the elephant in the room early on. It's like, "Hey, this may be a really cool product, but is this really the type of thing that you come back to?" And it's been incredible to not just see strong retention numbers, but just see an improvement in retention over time even as our cohorts become less of an early adopter and more the average person, so.
turns.zh: 显然，我能透露的具体信息十分有限，但确实我们的用户留存率数据令人振奋，而这正是我们最关注的核心指标。我们完全不在意用户在产品中停留的时长。实际上，我们的初衷就是解决用户的问题——只要你真心喜欢这款产品，就会选择订阅。但我们并无刻意留住用户的意图。不过，如果能在三个月甚至更长的时间里持续使用我们的产品，我们无疑会倍感欣喜。对我而言，这个问题在项目初期始终如同避重就轻的难题——人们总会问："这款产品确实很酷，但它真的值得用户反复回访吗？"令人欣喜的是，用户留存率不仅表现亮眼，而且随着用户群体从早期尝鲜者逐渐转变为普通用户，留存率数据还在持续攀升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So, that note is something that I don't think people truly understand how rare this is when a product... The cohort of users comes, tries it out and then retention over time goes down and then it comes back up, people come back to it a few months later and use it more. It's called a smiling curve, a smile curve, and that's extremely rare.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以，我觉得人们并没真正意识到这种情况有多罕见——当一款产品……用户群体先是尝试产品，接着留存率逐渐下降，然后又回升，几个月后用户重新回归并更加频繁地使用它。这被称为微笑曲线，而这种现象实属罕见。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Yeah. There's some smiling going on that's just on the team and I feel like have technology, some of it is not the product. I think people are actually just getting used to this technology in a really interesting way, where I find, and this is why the product needs to evolve too, that this idea of delegating to an AI, it's not natural to most people. It's not like you're going through life and figuring out what can I delegate? Certain sphere of Silicon Valley does that because they're in a self-optimization mode and they're trying to delegate everything they can. But I think for most people in the world it's actually quite unnatural. And you really have to learn, "Okay, what are my goals actually and what could another intelligence help me with?" (00:28:26): And I think that just takes time and people do figure it out once they've had enough time with the product. But then of course there's been tons of things that we've done in the product too, whether or not it's making the core models better, whether or not it's new capabilities like search and personalization and all that kind of stuff, or just standard growth work too, which we're starting to do. That stuff matters too, of course.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。对，团队里确实有一些微笑的互动。我觉得技术的应用有时并不能直接转化为产品本身。我认为人们实际上正在以一种非常有趣的方式适应这项技术。我发现——这也是产品需要不断进化的原因——将任务委托给人工智能的概念，对大多数人来说并不自然。毕竟，没有人会时时刻刻都在盘算自己能把哪些任务委托出去。硅谷的某些圈子会这样做，因为他们处于自我优化的模式，试图把一切都外包出去。但我认为对世界上大多数人来说，这确实不太习惯。你必须学会问自己："我的目标到底是什么？其他智能系统能帮我做些什么？"（00:28:26）。我认为这需要时间，当人们使用产品足够久后，自然会明白其中的门道。但当然，我们在产品上也做了大量改进——无论是优化核心模型，推出搜索、个性化等新功能，还是开展标准的增长优化工作（我们最近也开始着手这些工作）。这些改进同样至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you might be answering this question already, but let me just ask it directly. People may look at this and be like, "Okay, they're building this kind of layer on top of this God-like intelligence. Of course it will grow incredibly fast and retention will be incredible. What do you guys actually doing that sits on top of the model that makes it grow so fast and retain so much?" Is there something that has worked incredibly well that has moved metrics significantly that you can share?
turns.zh: 好吧，或许你们已经在回答这个问题了，但我还是直截了当地问一下。人们看到这个情况可能会想：“好吧，他们在这种神级智能之上构建了这样一层架构。当然它会增长得极快，用户留存率也会超高。但你们到底做了什么，能让模型在其之上实现如此快速的增长和高留存率呢？” 有没有什么特别有效的做法，能显著提升各项指标效果的，可以和我们分享一下？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: One thing we've learned, I'll answer that question in a minute, but one thing we've learned with ChatGPT is that there really is no distinction between the model and the product. The model is the product and therefore you need to iterate on it like a product. And by that I mean obviously you typically start by shipping something very open-ended, at least if you're OpenAI [inaudible 00:29:38] that's kind of a playbook. But then you really have to look at what are people trying to do? Okay, they're trying to write, they're trying to code, they're trying to get advice, they're trying to get recommendations and you need to systematically improve on those use cases. And that is pretty similar to product development work. Obviously the methodology is a bit different, but discovery is the same. You got to talk to people, you got to do data science and you got to try stuff and get feedback. (00:30:04): So, that's one chunk of work that we've been very consciously doing is improving the model on the use cases people care about. And there's also such thing as vibes because I'm sure you know and that's one of the things that I'm excited about in GPT-5 is that the vibes are really good. So, that too is, we have a model behavior team and they really focus on what is the personality of this model and how does it speak and talk. So, there's that kind of work. I would say that's maybe a third of the retention improvements that we see or so just roughly. And then I think another third is what I would call product research capabilities. They're research driven for sure. They have a research component, but they're really new product features or capabilities. And search is one example of that where if you remember in the olden days, maybe 20 months ago or something, you would talk to ChatGPT and it'd be like, "As of my knowledge cut off..." Or, "I can't answer that because that happened to recently," or something like that. (00:31:00): And that is the type of capability that has been incredibly retentive and for good reason. It just allows you to do more with the product personalization, like this idea of advanced memory where it can really get to know you over time is another example of a capability like that. I think that's another good chunk. And then the third stuff is the stuff you would do in any product and those things exist too. Not having to log in was a huge hit because it removed a ton of the friction. I think we had this intuition from the beginning, but we never got to it because we didn't have enough GPU or other constraint to really go do that. So, there's the traditional product work too. So, I often think about it as roughly a third, a third, a third, but really we're still learning and we're planning to evolve the product a ton, which is why I'm sure there's going to be new levers.
turns.zh: 有一件事我们已经意识到——我稍后会详细说明——但在ChatGPT上我们学到的一点是，模型和产品之间根本没有界限。模型本身就是产品，因此你需要像对待产品一样对其进行迭代。我的意思是，显然你通常会先推出一款非常开放的版本，至少如果你是OpenAI的话[00:29:38，语音不清]，这就是一种策略。但接下来你必须审视用户的实际需求：他们想写作、编程、寻求建议、获取推荐——你需要系统性地优化这些使用场景。这与产品开发的工作非常相似。当然，方法略有不同，但核心的探索思路是一致的：你需要与用户沟通、进行数据科学分析、不断尝试并收集反馈。（00:30:04）所以，我们一直在重点优化模型以满足用户关心的使用场景。这还涉及到所谓的“用户体验感”，相信大家都了解这一点。这也是我对GPT-5感到兴奋的原因之一——它的用户体验感确实很棒。因此，我们组建了模型行为团队，他们专注于模型的个性、表达方式等细节。这类工作占据了我们看到的用户留存提升效果的约三分之一。其次，我认为还有三分之一的改进来自于产品研究能力。这类工作本质上是以研究为导向的，包含研究部分，但更侧重于新产品功能或特性。搜索就是一个例子——回想20个月前左右的版本，当你与ChatGPT对话时，它会回应“根据我的现有知识……”，或者“我无法回答这个问题，因为这件事最近才发生”之类的话。这类功能的留存效果非常好，理由也很充分——它让产品个性化功能得以深度发挥。例如，先进的记忆功能能随着时间了解用户需求，这也是类似的能力提升。我认为这部分也很重要。第三部分是任何产品都会进行的常规工作——比如无需登录就可使用，这大大降低了用户门槛。我们从一开始就意识到这一点，但由于GPU资源不足等限制未能及时实现。因此，传统的产品优化工作同样重要。我常把改进分为三部分，但实际上我们仍在不断学习，计划对产品进行大量迭代，因此相信未来还会有新的优化方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned something that I want to come back to real quick. You said that it was something like 10 days from Hackathon to Sam tweeting about ChatGPT being live?
turns.zh: 你提到了一个情况，我想快速回顾一下。你说从黑客马拉松到萨姆（Sam）在推特上宣布ChatGPT正式上线，中间只隔了大约10天的时间？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: The Hackathon happened much earlier and we were prototyping for a long time, but at some point we basically ran out of patience on trying to build something more bespoke. And again, that was mostly because people always wanted to do all this other stuff whenever we tested it. So, it was 10 days from when we decided we were going to ship to when we shipped. And the research we'd been testing for a long time, it was kind of an evolution of what we'd called instruction following, which was the idea that instead of just completing the sentence, these models could actually follow you instructions. So, if you said summarize this, it would actually do so. And the research had evolved from that into a chat format where we could do it multi-turn. So, that research took way longer than 10 days and that kind of baking in the background, but the productization of this thing was very, very fast and lots of things didn't make it in. (00:32:50): I remember we didn't have history, which of course was the first user feedback we got. The model had a bunch of shortcomings and it was so cool to be able to iterate on the model. The thing I just talked about, treating the model as a product was not a thing before ChatGPT because we would ship in more hardware where there'd be a release GPT-3 and then we would start working on GPT-4 and these weird giant big spend R&D projects that would take a really long time and the spec was whatever the spec was and then you'd have to wait another year. And ChatGPT really broke that down because we were able to make iterative improvements to it just like software. And really, my dream is that it would be amazing if we could just ship daily or even hourly like in software land because you could just fix stuff, et cetera. But there's of course all kinds of challenges in how you do that while keeping the personality intact while not regressing other capabilities. So, it's an open field to get there.
turns.zh:
黑客马拉松结束得比较早，我们花了很长时间进行原型设计，但到了某个阶段，我们实在没耐心再去打造更定制化的功能了。说白了，主要是因为每次测试新功能时，总有人想尝试其他乱七八糟的玩法。最后，从决定上线到实际发布，整个过程只用了10天。我们长期测试的研究方向源于"指令跟随"技术——即让模型不仅能完成句子，还能根据用户指令进行操作。比如用户说"总结一下"，模型就能准确完成任务。后来，研究演化为多轮对话的聊天模式。但这项技术的研发远非10天之功，虽说在幕后持续打磨，但产品化进程却极其迅速，许多功能最终未能实现。

（00:32:50）我记得最初用户反馈最多的是缺少历史记录功能。模型存在诸多缺陷，但能快速迭代优化实在太棒了。我刚才提到的"将模型视为产品"这种理念，在ChatGPT出现之前是不可想象的。过去我们推出的都是硬件产品，比如GPT-3发布后，研发团队就开始着手GPT-4，整个研发周期漫长且规格僵化，要等上整整一年。而ChatGPT彻底打破了这种模式，我们可以像软件开发一样对模型进行迭代改进。

我的理想是能像软件行业那样每天甚至每小时发布更新——发现问题就及时修复。但要在保持个性化特性的同时不退化其他功能，挑战实在不小。这条路任重而道远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good example of is it maximally accelerated? Okay, we're going to ship ChatGPT 10 days.
turns.zh: 真是个绝佳的例子，它达到了最大加速效果吗？好的，我们计划在10天后正式发布ChatGPT。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: [inaudible 00:33:48]-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy moly. We've been talking about ChatGPT. Clearly it's kind of a chat interface. Everyone's always wondering is chat the future of all of this stuff? Interestingly, Kevin Weil made this really profound point that has always stuck with me when he was on the podcast that chat is actually a genius interface for building on a super intelligence because it's how we interact with humans of all variety of intelligence. It scales from someone at the lower end to a super smart person. And so, it's really valuable as a way to scale this spectrum. Maybe just talk about that and is chat the long-term interface for ChatGPT, I guess it's called ChatGPT.
turns.zh: 天哪，我们一直在讨论ChatGPT。显然它就是一个聊天界面啊，大家总在问——聊天会不会是所有这些技术的未来？有趣的是，Kevin Weil在播客上提出了一个让我印象深刻的深刻观点：聊天实际上是构建超级智能的绝佳界面，因为它是我们与不同智力水平的人类互动的方式。它能适配从智力水平较低的人，到超级聪明的个体。因此，作为拓展这个智能谱系的桥梁，它的价值非凡。或许我们可以聊聊这个话题——聊天会不会是ChatGPT（好吧，现在它叫GPT-4了）的长期交互界面呢？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I feel like we should either drop the chat or drop the GPT at some point because it is a mouthful. We're stuck with the name, but no matter what we do, the product will evolve. I think that I agree that there's something profound about natural language. It just really is the most natural form of communicating to humans and therefore it feels important that you should be communicating with your software in natural language. I think that's different from chat though. I think chat was the simplest way to ship at the time. I'm baffled by how much it took off as a concept. Even more baffled by how many people have copied the paradigm rather than trying out a different way of interacting with AI. I'm still hoping that will happen. So, I think natural language is here to stay, but this idea that it has to be a turn-by-turn chat interaction I think is really limiting. (00:35:24): And this is one of the reasons I don't love the super system analogy, even though we used to always use it is because if you think that way, then you kind of feel like you're talking to a person and GPT-5 it's amazing at making great front-end applications. So, I don't see a reason why you wouldn't have AIs that can render their own UI in some way. And you obviously want to make that predictable and feel good. But it feels limiting to me to think of the end-all-be-all interface as a chatbot. It actually kind of feels dystopian almost where I don't want to use all my software through the proxy of some interface. I love being in Figma, I love being in Google Docs. Those are all great products to me and they're not chatbots. (00:36:07): So, yes on natural language, but no on chat is where I would describe my point of view. And I'm just hoping in general that we see more consumer innovation on how people interact with AI because there's so many possibilities and you just got to try stuff. That's why chat stuck is we just did it and people liked it. So, I'm hoping that we see more there and we'll try to do our part.
turns.zh:
我觉得我们迟早得要放弃这个聊天界面，或者抛弃GPT模型，因为这个名字实在太冗长了。虽然我们现在不得不沿用这个名字，但无论如何产品都会不断迭代。我认同自然语言确实蕴含着深层价值——它是人类最自然的交流方式，因此用自然语言与软件交互至关重要。不过我认为这和传统聊天有本质区别。当时推出聊天功能只是最简单的实现方式。让我困惑的是，这个概念为何能如此火爆。更令人费解的是，众多厂商竞相复制这种范式，而不是探索与AI交互的新方式。我仍期待这种局面能有所改变。所以我认为自然语言会继续存在，但那种必须以回合制聊天形式呈现的观念实在太过局限。

（00:35:24）这也是我不喜欢超级系统类比的原因之一。虽然我们过去常用这个比喻，但若按这种思路思考，就会觉得是在和真人对话。GPT-5确实能出色地开发前端应用，但我看不出为何不让AI能自主渲染UI界面。显然我们希望界面交互既可预测又流畅。但把聊天机器人视为终极交互界面实在太过局限。这甚至让我产生反乌托邦的联想——我不想通过任何中间界面来使用所有软件。我喜欢Figma、Google Docs，这些产品都很棒，但它们都不是聊天机器人。

（00:36:07）所以我的观点是：支持自然语言，但反对聊天界面。我期待未来能看到更多消费者层面的AI交互创新，毕竟可能性无穷无尽，勇于尝试才是关键。如今聊天之所以能站稳脚跟，只是因为我们当时选择了简单易用的实现路径。希望未来能看到更多突破，我们也会尽自己的一份力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you mentioned that you kind of got stuck with this name ChatGPT. Maybe this is part of the answer, but I'm curious just are there any accidental decisions you guys made early on that have stuck and have essentially become history changing?
turns.zh: 嗯，你提到你们给这个项目取名时遇到了点困难，最后选定了ChatGPT这个名字。或许这只是其中一个原因，但我很好奇，你们早期是否曾做过一些看似随意的决定，最终却成了改变历史的关键节点？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: There's so many and it is funny, because you have no time to think about them and then they end up being super consequential. The day was one, we went from chat with GPT-3.5 to ChatGPT the night before, slightly better but still really bad.
turns.zh: 数量实在太多了，而且很有趣的是，你根本没时间仔细思考这些问题，最后它们却产生了巨大的影响。就拿今天来说吧，我们从前一天晚上还在用GPT-3.5聊天到现在改用ChatGPT，虽然有所改进，但整体效果还是很不理想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was it called before?
turns.zh: 它之前叫什么？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It was going to be Chat with GPT-3.5 because we really didn't think it was going to be successful product. We were trying to actually be as nerdy as we could about it because that's really what it was. It was a research demo, not a product. So, we didn't think that was bad. But I think that in the original release, making it free was a big deal. I don't think we appreciate that because the GPT-3.5 model was in our API for at least six months prior to that. I think anyone could have built something like this. It might not have been quite as good on the modeling side, but I think it would've taken off. So, making it free and putting a nice UI on it, very consequential in the way that you take for granted now. And this is why I think that A, distribution and the interface are continuously important even in 2025. (00:37:48): The paid business, which now it's a giant business both in the consumer space and in the enterprise space. The birth of that was just to turn away demand originally. It was not like we brainstormed, "Oh, what is the best monetization model for AI?" It was really what monetization model or what mechanism would allow us to turn away people who are less serious than the people who are really trying to use it? And subscriptions just happened to have that property and it grew into a large business. I think shipping really funky capabilities before they were polished is another thing where that feels like a tactical decision, but it became a playbook because we would learn so much. Remember when we shipped Code Interpreter, we learned so much after we shipped it. Now it's known as I think data analysis in ChatGPT or something like that just because we actually got real world use cases back that we could then optimize. So, I think there's been a lot of decisions over time that proved pretty consequential, but we made them very, very quickly as we have to, so.
turns.zh:
原本我们打算推出GPT-3.5的聊天功能，因为我们真心不认为它能成为成功的产品。我们当时试图尽可能地保持技术细节的严谨性，因为这本质上就是一个研究演示品，而非成熟的产品。所以我们并不觉得这有什么不妥。但我认为在最初发布时，将其免费开放确实意义重大。如今回想起来，我们可能没有充分意识到这一点，因为GPT-3.5模型在我们的API中已经存在了至少六个月。任何人都能开发出类似的产品，尽管在模型质量上可能稍逊一筹，但我相信它同样会引发热潮。因此，免费开放并赋予其友好的用户界面，这在如今看来是理所当然的成功之举。但这恰恰说明，2025年及以后的时代里，产品分发与用户界面仍将是至关重要的核心竞争力。

（00:37:48）付费业务如今已发展为消费者与企业领域的巨头。但最初推出付费服务只是为了应对过载需求。当时我们并未刻意设计"最佳AI变现模式"，而是探讨了这样一个问题：如何筛选出那些缺乏专业性的用户，让真正有需求的客户能够顺利使用？订阅模式恰好具备这样的筛选功能，最终成长为庞大业务。

在功能尚未完善时就急于上线，这看似是一种战术性决策，但事实证明它已成为最佳实践。例如，推出代码解析器后，我们从用户反馈中获得了大量优化建议，最终将其融入ChatGPT的数据分析功能。这种快速试错的策略，让我们在产品迭代中不断积累经验，形成良性循环。

总之，许多看似随意的决策最终都产生了深远影响。我们必须在极短时间内做出这些决策，未来也将继续秉持这种敏捷创新精神。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The $20 a month feels like an important part of this. Feels like everybody's just doing that now and-
turns.zh: 每月20美元的费用，感觉这对整个计划至关重要。感觉现在每个人都在这么做，而且...

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: On that one actually, I remember I had this kind of panic attack because we really needed to launch subscriptions because at the time we were taking the product down every time. It was, I don't know if you remember, we had this fail whale, there's a little [inaudible 00:39:09] generated poem on it. So, they were like, "We had to get this out." And I remember calling up someone I greatly respect who's incredible at pricing and I was like, "What should I do?" And we talked a bunch and I just ran out of time to incorporate most of that feedback. So, what I did do is ship a Google Form to Discord with, I think the four questions you're supposed to ask on how to price something-
turns.zh: 关于这件事，我记得当时自己陷入了恐慌状态，因为我们确实急需推出订阅服务，而当时我们每次都要下架产品。不知道你是否还记得，当时我们遇到了那个“故障鲸鱼”（fail whale），还有用户为此创作的打油诗。他们当时急着要把产品上线，我记得我打电话给一位我非常尊敬的定价专家，问他：“我该怎么办？”我们聊了很久，但最后我实在来不及把大部分建议都融入到产品中。所以我最后的做法是，把谷歌表单发送到Discord平台，里面包含了四个关于定价策略的核心问题——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:39:32]?

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. It literally had those four questions and I remember distinctly A, you [inaudible 00:39:38] a price back and that's kind of how we got to $20. But B, the next morning, there was a press article on you won't believe the four genius questions the ChatGPT team asked to price their... It was like if only you knew. So, there's something about building in this extreme public where people interpret so much more intentionality into what you're doing than might've actually existed at the time. But we got with the $20. We're debating something slightly higher at the time. I often wonder what would've happened because so many other companies ended up copying the $20 price point. So, I'm like, "Did we erase a bunch of market cap by pressing it this way?" But ultimately I don't care because the more accessible we can make this stuff, the better. And I think this is the price point that in Western countries has been reasonable to a lot of people in terms of the value that they get back. (00:40:27): And most importantly, we were able to push things down to the free tier semi-regularly and we always do that when we can [inaudible 00:40:35], but-
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。当时就四个问题，我记得很清楚。第一个问题，你（00:39:38处语音不清）给出了一个价格，这就是我们最终定价20美元的关键。但第二天早上，媒体报道称"你绝对想不到ChatGPT团队为了定价问了四个天才问题"。当时要是你知道就好了。在这样极度透明的公众视野下，你的一举一动都会被放大解读，人们会赋予你比当时实际更多的主观意图。不过最终我们还是定价20美元了。当时我们还在考虑稍微提高一点价格。我常想如果当初定价更高会怎样，毕竟很多其他公司最后都复制了20美元这个定价点。我甚至会想"我们是不是因为这样定价而错失了大量市值？"但说实话我并不在乎，因为让产品更亲民才是最重要的。我认为这个定价在西方国家对于大多数用户来说，已经足够合理地体现了他们所获得的价值。（00:40:27）最重要的是，我们能定期将价格下调至免费层级，每当条件允许时我们都会这么做，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the survey, just to give the official name, the Van Westendorp survey is how you guys ended up pricing ChatGPT?
turns.zh: So, the survey, just to give the official name, the Van Westendorp survey is how you guys ended up pricing ChatGPT?

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It was the top Google result. This was before ChatGPT has real-time information. Otherwise, it could have maybe price itself, but it was Discord plus Google Form plus a blog post on that methodology that got us there.
turns.zh: 它是谷歌搜索结果的首条推荐。这是在ChatGPT尚未掌握实时信息的时期，否则它或许能自行定价。但最终我们是通过Discord、Google表单以及一篇关于该方法的博客文章才成功做到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is incredible. What a fun story. This is the survey that Rahul Vohra at Superhuman popularized in his first- round article-
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。真是个有趣的故事。这就是Rahul Vohra在《超人》杂志首轮文章中推广的调查报告。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, yeah, that's right. That's right. Definitely don't bring me on here as a pricing expert, I think you have got better people for that.
turns.zh: 是啊。对，对，对，没错。绝对别把我请来当定价专家，我觉得你们有更合适的人选来做这件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whether it was right or wrong, it is now the fastest-growing, insane revenue generating business in the world. So, I wouldn't feel too bad.
turns.zh: 无论这件事是对是错，如今它已然是全球增长最快、创收最疯狂的行业。所以，我倒不觉得这有多糟糕。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: No, it worked out. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错，事情进展得很顺利。太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It worked out. And by the way, I'm on the $200 a month tier, so there's clearly a room-
turns.zh: 结果还不错。顺便说一下，我现在每月支付200美元的费用层级，所以显然还有提升空间——

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Thank you. Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: The story of that one is interesting too because originally the purpose of the Plus plan was to be able to ship first uptime and then be able to ship capabilities that we couldn't scale to everyone. And at some point it got so many people in the Plus tier that had just lost that property. So, the main reason we came up with the $200 tier is just we had so much incredible research that's actually really, really powerful. Like o3 Pro or tomorrow GPT-5 Pro and just having a vehicle of shipping that to people who really, really care is exciting even though it kind of violates the standard way a SaaS page should look, it's a little jarring to see the 10X jump. So, thank you for being a subscriber on that and thank you everyone else who's watching you subscribed to any tier, it's great.
turns.zh: 那个故事也很有趣，因为最初Plus计划的目的是先推出核心功能，然后再逐步向所有用户开放高级功能。然而后来Plus层级用户数量激增，导致部分用户失去了这一特权。因此，我们推出200美元付费层级的核心原因在于，我们掌握了极其宝贵的研究成果——比如o3 Pro、即将推出的GPT-5 Pro等——而通过这种方式将这些强大功能推送给真正有需求的用户，既令人兴奋又充满挑战。虽然这种定价策略与SaaS页面标准设计相悖，但当用户看到价格跳升10倍时难免会感到意外。感谢订阅该层级的用户，也感谢所有观看视频并订阅任一层级的观众，感谢你们的支持！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm just going to throw a fishing line into this pond of are there any other stories like this? You shared this incredible story of Chat with GPT-3.5 being the original name, how you came up with pricing. Is there anything else?
turns.zh: 我就随便抛个问题，问问大家有没有类似的经历？你分享了那个超棒的故事，讲的是ChatGPT 3.5最初的名字，还有你怎么定价的。还有其他故事吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Enterprise is interesting one too because we've seen so much incredible adoption in the Enterprise and it's sort of objectively crazy to try to take on building a developer business and a consumer business and an enterprise business and all at once. But the story there is in like month one or two, it was very clear that most of the usage was work usage, actually much more than today where you've got so many consumers on the product and it's kind of sort of transcended into pop culture. But at the time it was writing, coding, analysis, that kind of stuff. And we were pretty quickly in organically in 90% of Fortune 500 companies in a way that I had seen maybe at Dropbox back when that was my two jobs ago where we had a similar story. And since then there's been more PLG companies. But the real reason we did Enterprise, remember we were debating should we do enterprise or should we launch an iOS app because that's how small the team was. (00:43:22): The reason we did is we were starting to get banned in companies because they all felt rightfully or wrongfully that the privacy and deployment story, et cetera wasn't there. So, I was just like, "Man, we have to do something. We're going to miss out on a generational opportunity to build a work product." And we've literally defined AGI as outperforming most humans at economically valuable work or I'd probably [inaudible 00:43:45] that, but I think that's the way we put it. And so, I feel like we had to be present there and it was a fairly quick decision at the time, but it's grown into an immense business. We just hit 5 million business subscribers up from 3 million, I think a month or two ago. So, it is kind of the spinoff that it's taking a life of its own that I'm really, really excited about for [inaudible 00:44:11]-
turns.zh: 企业业务也很有趣，因为我们在企业领域见证了令人惊叹的用户增长。试图同时构建面向开发者、消费者和企业的业务组合，客观上确实有些疯狂。但早在一两个月时，我们就清楚地发现，大多数用户场景都是工作场景——这远超如今产品已渗透到众多消费者群体、甚至成为流行文化标杆的阶段。当时用户主要使用产品进行编程、分析等工作。在不到一年的时间里，我们就自然渗透进90%的《财富》500强企业，这让我想起两年前在Dropbox工作的经历，当时我们也面临过类似的挑战。此后更多PLG（订阅制）公司涌现。但最初选择企业业务的真正原因，是我们当时在纠结是专注企业还是推出iOS应用——毕竟当时团队规模很小。（00:43:22）最终我们选择了企业业务，因为很多公司开始封禁我们的产品。他们认为我们的隐私保护、部署管理等功能存在不足——无论这种担忧是否合理。我们当时就想："天哪，我们必须采取行动，否则将错过打造办公产品的千载难逢良机。"我们曾将AGI定义为在经济价值高的工作场景中超越大多数人类的表现——虽然现在可能调整了表述，但核心理念始终如一。因此，我们必须布局企业市场。当时的决策速度很快，如今这项业务已发展为庞然大物。就在一两个月前，我们的企业用户数从300万攀升至500万。这项业务正以势不可挡的势头独立发展，这让我倍感振奋[00:44:11]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a lot to be handling the platform essentially the API, the consumer product, the fastest-growing, most successful product in history and also the B2B side, which is clearly a massive business. Do you have any kind of heuristics for how to make these trade-offs do all this at once and stay sane and be successful?
turns.zh: 处理这个平台实在是太难了——要管API、消费者产品、史上增长最快、最成功的产品，还要兼顾B2B业务，这显然是一项庞大的事业。你们有没有什么诀窍，能在面对诸多挑战时做出取舍，同时保持理智并取得成功呢？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: That's a good question. And first off, I don't run the developer stuff anymore. We found someone way more competent to do that and he's amazing. So, I still look after the various forms of chat, but luckily you don't have to make that trade-off OpenAI does. And I can get into that too, but it keeps me a little bit more sane. I will say that you kind of have to practice in two different ways when you're building on this AI stuff. One is sort of working backwards from the model capabilities and that is much more art than science, where I think you really need to look at what tech do we have available and what is the most awesome way to productize it? And if you applied to some sort of PM framework to that, I think you would do something horrible wrong. Because if you have tech that's, for example, GPT-5 is really, really good at front-end coding now, I think that means you've got to reprioritize it. (00:45:27): You got to actually bring that capability to life. Maybe that's making ChatGPT better at vibe coding and rendering applications. Maybe that's more like leveraging the taste of the model to make the UI more expressive. There's a number of things we could do, but you kind of have to replan and reprioritize and that is more important than any particular audience segmentation. It's really just looking at what is the magic thing we have and how do you make it shine. Voice is a similar thing. It wasn't like our customers need voice, they're begging for it or something like that. It was like, "Wow, we figured out a way how to make these things anything in, anything out." What is a creative awesome way to productize that and then we can see what people do. So, I think that's one chunk of it. But then the other chunk of it really is more like classic product management where you need to listen to customers and then when your customers are really different, that can be confusing because ChatGPT is a very general purpose product. (00:46:23): We see when you look at end users, there's actually an immense amount of overlap in terms of what they want. Primitives like projects or history search or sharing and collaboration, all those kinds of things. They are actually very, very present. Whether or not you're talking to people at work or you're talking to people at home, at school, there's slightly different mechanics sometimes, but they're largely similar investments that I think we can get a lot of mileage out of. And then there's Enterprise-specific work that we just have to do. You've got to do HIPAA, you got to do SOC 2, you've got to do all those things if you want to be a serious player. And those are just non-negotiable. So, it's complex as you correctly identified, but it's kind of the curse of working on a very open-ended and powerful technology. (00:47:11): One analogy that someone at OpenAI who I really respect, he's like, "We're kind of like Disney, where Disney has this one kind of creative IP, which is their content, and they have cruises and they have theme parks and they have comics and they have all these different things." And I think we have amazing models, but there's all these different ways that you can productize them and we kind of just have to maximize the impact in all these different ways.
turns.zh:
嗯，这是个好问题。但首先，我现在已经不再负责开发团队的工作了。我们找到了一个更胜任的人来接手，他做得非常出色。所以，我现在主要负责各种形式的聊天功能，不过好在你们不必像OpenAI那样面临同样的权衡取舍。我可以详细讲讲这个，但这样能让我保持清醒一些。我得说，在基于AI技术进行开发时，确实需要两种不同的思维方式。一种是从模型能力倒推，这更多是艺术而非科学。在这种情况下，你需要审视现有技术，思考如何以最酷的方式将其产品化。如果用传统的PM框架来处理，恐怕会走入歧途。比如说，GPT-5现在在前端编码方面表现得非常出色，这意味着你必须重新调整优先级。（00:45:27）你得真正把这项能力落地——或许是让ChatGPT更擅长前端编码和渲染应用程序，或许是利用模型的洞察力让UI更具表现力。我们可以有很多尝试，但关键在于重新规划和调整优先级，这比任何特定的用户细分都重要。关键在于审视现有技术的神奇之处，并想办法让它大放异彩。语音功能也是类似的情况。用户并不是急切需要语音功能，而是我们发现了如何让这些技术实现双向转换的解决方案。如何以创新的方式将其产品化，然后观察用户反应。这就是其中一部分。但另一部分更像是传统的产品管理——你需要倾听用户需求，而当用户群体差异巨大时，挑战就来了。ChatGPT是一款通用型产品。（00:46:23）从终端用户角度看，需求有大量重叠部分。比如项目管理、历史记录搜索、共享与协作等基础功能，这些在不同场景下可能有所差异，但核心需求高度一致。无论是职场场景还是家庭场景，底层逻辑大同小异，值得深挖。当然，针对企业级客户的合规要求（如HIPAA、SOC 2）也是必不可少的。正如你所指出的，这确实很复杂，但这也是基于开放式、强大技术进行开发的必然挑战。

（00:47:11）OpenAI的一位我非常尊敬的同事曾打比方说：“我们就像迪士尼，迪士尼拥有一种核心创意IP——内容创作，同时还经营游轮、主题公园、漫画等多元业务。”我们也拥有卓越的模型，但如何将其转化为产品，确实需要多管齐下、深挖潜力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you were talking, I was thinking about how usually horizontal platforms that are just so general and can do so much take a long time to take off because people don't know what to do with them. They're not amazing at anything. And this is an amazing counter example where it took off immediately and everyone figured it out and then over time they figured it out more and more.
turns.zh: 你说话的时候，我一直在想，通常那些功能过于笼统、功能繁多的横向平台之所以难以推广，是因为人们不知道该如何利用它们。它们在任何特定领域都表现平平。但这个案例却是个惊人的反例——它一上线就迅速走红，用户很快掌握了使用方法，随着时间推移，用户的使用水平也不断提升。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: But I think the reason why is because it just went live. Talk about another consequential decision actually. We were debating waitlist, no waitlist because we-
turns.zh: 但我觉得原因在于它刚刚上线了。说到这儿，倒是另一个重大的决策。我们之前一直在讨论是否要设置候补名单，最终决定不设名单，因为我们...

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Actually we were debating waitlist/no waitlist because we really knew we couldn't scale the engineering systems. And the fact that there was no waitlist, which no open AI release had worked like that before, ended up being consequential because you were able to watch what everyone else was doing live. So I think when you launch these things all at once for everyone, there really is a special moment where you can see what other people are doing and learn from that. (00:48:25): And a lot of that is actually out of product. There's these crazy TikTok posts that go viral and they have like 2, 000 use cases in the comments. And I go through those in detail because it's not like I knew about those use cases either. They're very, very emergent and I just go through the comments and process because there's so much to learn. And for that reason, I think we get to skip the empty box problem a little bit because so much learning is happening out of product as people are watching each other either in IRL or online.
turns.zh:
实际上，我们当时正在讨论是否采用候补名单机制，因为我们深知工程系统无法承受大规模扩容压力。由于此前没有任何开放式人工智能产品采用这种机制，这一设计最终产生了深远影响——用户能够实时观察其他人的操作行为。正因如此，我认为当所有用户同时上线新功能时，会形成一个特殊的学习时刻，让人们得以观察他人的实践并从中获益。

（00:48:25）这其中很多灵感并非来自产品团队本身。TikTok上曾有一些疯狂的帖子迅速走红，评论区涌现出2000个应用场景案例。我会仔细研究这些案例，因为我原本对这些应用场景也一无所知。这些案例具有很强的创新性，于是我会逐条分析评论，学习其中的精华。正因如此，我认为我们能在一定程度上避免"空白盒子问题"（empt box problem），因为用户无论是线下交流还是在线互动，都能通过观察彼此的实践获得大量学习机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting because you think about Airtable, you think about Notion, all these companies, they took years to just build and craft and think and go deep on what it could be.
turns.zh: 这真是太有趣了。因为一提到Airtable、Notion这些公司，你会发现它们都花费了数年时间进行研发、打磨产品，深入思考其潜在价值所在。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It's like they compare Airtable, which they had to do templates, they had to do all these kind of things of taking the horizontal product and making it use case driven. They compare it to the Instant Pot, which there's recipes being shared everywhere online. There's this whole ecosystem around it. I think we were really lucky with ChatGPT that that happened where there's just users sharing use cases with other users everywhere. And therefore I think we got very lucky by jumping ahead on that journey.
turns.zh: 这就好比他们把Airtable和Instant Pot作比较——前者需要手动制作模板，处理各种复杂的横向产品功能，后者则能让用户轻松分享食谱，围绕其形成完整的生态系统。我觉得我们在ChatGPT上运气特别好，因为它天然具备用户之间互相分享应用场景的功能。正因如此，我们能在这场技术革命中抢占先机，真是太幸运了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like a quarter there is Sam had big following and everyone would pay attention to something you launch. So that's a really interesting new strategy for launching horizontal product. With a huge distribution channel, just launch it and see what comes up.
turns.zh: 感觉在Quora上有个叫Sam的用户粉丝众多，每当你推出新产品时，大家都会给予关注。这对于横向产品发布而言，确实是一项极具吸引力的新策略。凭借庞大的分发渠道，直接上线产品，看看市场反响如何再做调整。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. And of course I'm actually really excited to take some of that into the product. I think we shouldn't rest on the fact that there's so much out product discovery happening. I actually think for the average consumer, it would be amazing if the product did a little bit more work on really exposing to you what is possible. (00:50:07): I still feel like ChatGPT feels a little bit like MS-DOS, like we haven't built Windows yet. And it'll be obvious once we do, but there's something that feels a little bit like... Imagine MS-DOS had gone viral and you were just trying to hack little conversation starters onto it. That might've missed sort of the big picture in terms of how to really communicate affordances and value to people. And so I think there's actually a ton more product work to do in addition to just seeing use cases spread.
turns.zh: 是的。当然，我真的很兴奋能将其中一些成果融入产品中。我认为，我们不应满足于现有产品发现功能的现状。对我而言，如果产品能在向用户清晰展示其潜力方面下更多功夫，那对普通消费者来说无疑会是件好事。（00:50:07）我仍觉得ChatGPT有点像MS-DOS系统，仿佛我们还未开发出Windows操作系统。等我们真正完成开发后，差距就会显而易见，但目前仍存在一些不足之处……想象一下，如果MS-DOS系统突然走红，而你只是一味地在其基础上拼凑一些简陋的聊天小工具，这或许会错失向用户传达产品功能与价值的关键机遇。因此，我认为除了推广应用场景外，还需要在产品设计上投入更多精力，才能真正让用户领略到其真正的潜力与价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you able to share just what you think that might look like? This Windows version of ChatGPT?
turns.zh: 你能分享一下你认为这个Windows版的ChatGPT可能会是什么样子吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I'll let you know when we figure it out. We're hiring. I think there's so many interesting product problems here.
turns.zh: 等我们弄清楚了再告诉你。我们正在招人。我觉得这里有很多有趣的产品难题需要解决。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, got it. By the way, I also love that TikTok was like your feedback channel.
turns.zh: 好的，我明白了。顺便说一句，我也很欣赏TikTok充当你反馈渠道的这个角色。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Those common threads, they're just so wild. And also the love that people have for it, the excitement with which you're sharing their product, I feel like it's special that people are so excited to share what they're doing with your product. And I don't take that for granted either.
turns.zh: 那些共通的元素真是太不可思议了。还有人们对它的热爱，以及你们分享他们产品时所洋溢的激情——我觉得人们能如此兴奋地用你们的产品展示自己的成果，这实在是太特别了。而我也从不把这视为理所当然。
