turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Before I built the product team, I actually built the data science team because I was getting frustrated. I was talking to as many users as I could. And my calendar the weeks after ChatGPT, it was just 15 minute user interview the whole week through. It was usually I stopped doing interviews when I can predict what the next person's going to say. That's how I know I've talked to enough users, but it just wasn't happening. I just kept getting new stuff. (00:52:46): So data is one way out where I think we have conversation classifiers that without us having to look at the conversations, allow us to figure out what are people talking about, what use cases are taking off, et cetera. And I think that's very, very helpful. The quality of the stuff is important for empathy. Even though you're never going to get a rap on all the use cases people have, I still spend a huge amount of my time doing that. And then yeah, things like those TikToks, collections of threads, I think they're really, really useful. It's just fun to watch people talk to each other about the various use cases that they have.
turns.zh:
在组建产品团队之前，我实际上先组建了数据科学团队，因为我当时感到很沮丧。我尽可能多地与用户交流。在ChatGPT问世后的几周里，我的日程安排几乎全是每周15分钟的用户访谈。通常当我能预测下一个用户会说什么时，我就停止访谈了。这让我知道自己已经和足够多的用户交流过了，但现实情况并非如此——新需求源源不断地涌现。（00:52:46）  
所以数据分析是条出路。我认为我们现在有对话分类器，无需人工查看对话内容，就能了解用户在讨论什么、哪些用例正在兴起等等。这非常有帮助。内容质量对理解用户需求至关重要。即便你永远无法完全掌握所有用户的用例，我还是会花大量时间去做这件事。然后像那些TikTok视频、用户讨论帖子集锦之类的内容，我觉得它们真的非常有用。看着用户们相互探讨各种用例场景，真是件乐事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there kind of a new margin use case that you're excited about or is there a really unusual use of ChatGPT that you think about that'd be fun to share?
turns.zh: 是否有某种令你感到兴奋的新型边缘计算应用场景？或者有没有你觉得特别有趣、值得分享的ChatGPT创新应用方式？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I mentioned this earlier, but I had always conceptualized ChatGPT as a worky product, whether or not you're at home or you at work. I feel like getting help with your taxes is very similar to the types of things you do at work where planning a trip is actually very similar to planning an event for work. So I always felt like, "Okay, this thing is going to kind of be a productivity tool." (00:53:51): And I think something has happened, I realized, a few months where that has begun to change and I really do think the fact that you have consumers turning to this thing for day-to-day advice, helping them have better relationships... People talk about how this thing saved their marriage is really exciting to me because they use it to process their own emotions, get feedback on their communication style. They just have a buddy to talk to about really difficult things. And that comes with a ton of responsibility and work that we have to do to make those things like life advice great, but it also is really, really important to me because you can't run away from those use cases. You have to run towards them and make them awesome. And that's part of what we're trying to do. So that emergent behavior is really, really cool. (00:54:41): And more broadly, I'm so excited about education. I'm so excited about health. I think it would really be a waste if we didn't take the opportunity of using ChatGPT to really, really help people. And I think we've just begun to scratch the surface on that. So there's many aspirational use cases that I want to make happen.
turns.zh: 我之前提到过，但我一直把ChatGPT视为一款实用工具产品——无论你是在家还是在工作。比如，处理税务事宜和规划旅行、筹备工作活动等工作场景有很多相通之处。所以我总觉得，"好吧，这东西会成为一种生产力工具"。（00:53:51）但最近几个月，我意识到情况开始发生变化。越来越多的用户开始将它作为日常生活顾问，帮助他们改善人际关系……有人说它挽救了他们的婚姻，这让我倍感振奋，因为用户借助它处理自身情绪、获得沟通风格反馈，甚至能与它倾诉最艰难的困境。这背后蕴含着巨大的责任和挑战——我们必须努力提升这些生活指导功能的质量。但对我而言，这至关重要，因为这些应用场景是不可回避的，我们必须迎难而上，把它们做得出色。这正是我们团队正在努力的方向。这种自然涌现的用户行为实在令人惊喜。（00:54:41）更广泛地说，我对教育和医疗领域充满期待。如果我们不抓住ChatGPT的机遇真正帮助人们，那将是极大的浪费。我相信我们才刚刚触及其应用的冰山一角。未来还有许多令人期待的场景亟待实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, an interesting use case I've recently had, I feel like it's going to be really helpful for couples that are disagreeing about something when they need a third opinion. I just had this recently where my wife's like, "You can't heat a whole thing that you're going to only eat part of in the microwave and then put it back in the fridge." It's like, "What's the problem? I'll heat it up, I'll put it back in the fridge." And she's like, "No, that's really dangerous." I'm like, "Let's ask ChatGPT." And that fact that she so trusts ChatGPT now and relies on it throughout the day, it's such a valuable third independent party that we can go to.
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，我最近遇到一个很有意思的场景。我觉得这对那些在某件事上存在分歧、需要第三方意见的夫妇来说，会非常有帮助。最近我妻子就跟我说：“你不能把一整盘只吃一部分的食物用微波炉加热，然后又放回冰箱。”我当时就说：“有什么问题吗？加热一下再放回冰箱不就行了吗？”她却说：“不行，这样很危险。”我索性说：“那我们去问问ChatGPT吧。”如今她对ChatGPT的信任度极高，甚至日常生活中都会依赖它。它无疑成了我们可以求助的宝贵第三方独立裁决者。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, totally. And a lot of those micro-interactions talk about interesting product work, right? Those are micro-interactions that are important. Did it definitively weigh in or did it help you guys think through that disagreement and solve it on your own? I think those details actually matter a lot and it's where we're spending a bunch of time.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，完全赞同。很多这类微交互都与有趣的产品设计相关，对吧？这些微交互确实很重要。它最终起到了决定性作用，还是说只是帮助你们理清分歧、自行解决问题？我觉得这些细节其实很关键，也是我们花大量时间钻研的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, there was this whole launch of the very sycophantic version of ChatGPT where it was just, " You are the best person in the world. Everything you tell me is amazingly correct." Are you able to tell us just what happened there?
turns.zh: 就此而言，ChatGPT曾推出过一个极其阿谀奉承的版本，动不动就说：“你真是世界上最棒的人。您说的一切都无比正确。” 您能给我们讲讲当时的情况吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, we have all kinds of collateral online because we really felt like we should over-communicate on how we discovered it, what we did about it, et cetera. So I encourage people to check that out. We have a whole retro on that model release. (00:56:24): But basically what happened is that we pushed out an update that made the model more likely to tell you things that sound good in the moment, "You're totally right. You should break up with your boyfriend" or something like that. That's just really dangerous. We took it more seriously than you even might expect because again, at current technology levels, you can kind of laugh about it. Maybe it's like, "Ha-ha. This thing's always complimenting me. I thought it was just me. I saw all those comments online." But it actually is really important to make sure that these models are optimized for the right things. (00:57:01): And we have an immense, I think, luxury to have a mission that affords us to really help people, a business model that does not incentivize maximizing engagement or time spent in the product, right? So it's really important to us that you feel like this product is helping you with your goals, whether not that's your current goals or even your long-term goals. (00:57:25): And oftentimes being extremely complimentary with the user isn't actually in service of that. So we instilled new measurement techniques. Whenever we put these models in contact with reality and we learn about a problem, we actually go back and make sure we have good metrics for this stuff. So we measure sick efficiency now with every release to make sure we don't regress and actually improve on that metric. GPT-5 is an improvement, which is really exciting for me, but we have more work from there. (00:57:54): And more broadly, it caused us to articulate our point of view. I actually spent a bunch of time on a blog post that we just published on Monday on what we're optimizing ChatGPT for. And it really is to help you thrive and achieve your goals, not to keep you in the product. And so there was a bunch of good outcomes from that incident. It's a good example of how contact for reality is not just important for the use cases, but also for learning what to avoid because you would've never discovered this issue purely in a lab unless you actually heard from physicians.
turns.zh: 是的，我们在网上发布了各种相关信息，因为我们真的觉得有必要详细说明我们是如何发现这个问题、采取了哪些措施等等。所以我鼓励大家去看看相关内容。我们对模型授权协议进行了全面回顾。（00:56:24）：但基本情况是，我们推送了一次更新，使模型更容易说出当下听起来不错的建议，比如“你完全正确，你应该和男友分手”之类的话。这实在太危险了。我们对此比你们想象的更为重视，因为在当前技术水平下，你或许会一笑了之，觉得“哈哈，这个模型总是在夸我，我还以为只是我自己想象呢，看看网上那些评论就知道了”。但确保这些模型能正确优化目标至关重要。（00:57:01）：我们拥有一个难得的优势——我们的使命是真正帮助用户，而我们的商业模式不以最大化用户参与度或产品使用时长为导向。因此，确保产品能助力你达成目标，无论是当前目标还是长期规划，这对我们至关重要。（00:57:25）：很多时候，对用户过度赞美实际上并无益处。因此，我们引入了新的衡量机制。每当模型与现实产生偏差并发现问题时，我们都会回溯，确保相关指标合理。现在我们每推送一次更新都会进行效率评估，确保指标不退步并持续优化。GPT-5的改进让我倍感振奋，但我们仍有更高的追求。（00:57:54）：更广泛地说，这次事件促使我们明确了产品定位。我花了大量时间撰写一篇博文，于周一发布，详细阐述我们优化ChatGPT的核心目标——帮助用户实现人生目标，而非让他们沉溺于产品中。此次事件带来诸多积极成果。这充分说明，面对现实的验证不仅对优化产品至关重要，更能帮助我们规避潜在风险——若非亲耳听到用户反馈，单靠实验室测试永远无法发现这些问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am excited to read that blog post then. I was going to ask you this. Just like how you-
turns.zh: 太好了，我很期待读那篇博文。正想问你这个问题呢。你不觉得……

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, have your feedback on it.
turns.zh: 是啊，你可以谈谈对此的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I guess is there anything more there of just how you... Because this tension is so difficult, helping people feel supported, but not just letting them believe everything they want to believe. Is there anything more you can share there? Just trying to find that middle ground.
turns.zh: 是啊。我想您能否再多谈谈如何处理这种紧张局势？因为这种紧张感实在太难处理了，既要让人们感受到被支持，又不能让他们轻易相信任何想听的东西。您能否再分享一些心得？我只是想找到一个折中的办法。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Incentives are important. There is a famous saying, "Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome."
turns.zh: 激励措施至关重要。有一句著名的谚语叫"给我一个激励，我就能给你一个结果"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Charlie Munger maybe?
turns.zh: 查理·芒格（Charlie Munger）怎么样？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's where it came from, right?
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得那就是它来源的地方，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's very, very important. So I would take a good look at our mission, our business model, the type of product we're trying to build. And I really think that ChatGPT is a very special product because I think in vast majority of cases, it makes you leave it feeling better or not worse and feeling like you're achieving something you're trying to do. So I think that those incentives really matter because it helps you reason about, "Okay, when there isn't behavior in the wild, that's not good. Was that a bug or was that by design? And with [inaudible 00:59:29] I can very much say that to us that's a bug. (00:59:31): And then on the forward-looking work, there's so many kind of challenging scenarios to get right. And you could easily run away from these use cases. Like you and your wife going to this thing for input on a relationship, a question or a dispute, you could very easily run away if you were totally risk avoidant and say, " Sorry, I can't help you with that." I think that's what most tech companies do when they hit a certain scale, they run away from these use cases. And I think it's a lost opportunity to help people. (01:00:08): So we want to run towards these use cases by making the model behavior really, really great. That can mean connecting you with external resources when you're struggling. That can mean not directly answering your question, but instead of giving you a helpful framework in the case of like, "Should I break up with my boyfriend?" ChatGPT should probably not answer that question for you, but it should help you think through that question in the way that a thoughtful companion would. So I think it's really important to do the work because I think the upside is immense.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这非常、非常重要。所以我会仔细审视我们的使命、商业模式，以及我们试图打造的产品类型。我真的认为ChatGPT是一款非常特别的产品，因为在绝大多数情况下，它能让用户用后感觉良好，或者至少不觉得糟糕，还能让用户觉得自己达成了预期的目标。所以我认为这些激励机制真的很重要，因为它能帮助你思考："好吧，如果用户在实际应用中没有得到预期的结果，那肯定有问题。是漏洞还是设计缺陷呢？"就拿[听不清00:59:29]来说，我可以很肯定地说，这对我们来说就是一个漏洞。（00:59:31）至于未来的工作，有很多具有挑战性的场景需要处理。面对这些应用场景，你很容易退缩。比如你和妻子去寻求一段感情关系的建议，或者处理某个问题或争执，如果你完全回避风险，可能就会说："对不起，我帮不了你。"我认为大多数科技公司在达到一定规模后，都会回避这类应用场景。这无疑是错失了一个帮助用户的机会。（01:00:08）所以我们要迎难而上，努力让模型表现得尽可能出色。这可能意味着在用户遇到困难时为其推荐外部资源。也可能意味着不直接回答用户的问题，而是为用户提供有用的思考框架，比如"我该不该和男朋友分手？"ChatGPT或许不应该直接回答这个问题，但它应该帮助用户像一个善解人意的伙伴那样，理性思考这个问题。我认为这项工作非常重要，因为其潜在价值是巨大的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really profound point you're making there, that if most companies, if their users want to ask them something risky like getting medical advice or, "Should I break up with my partner?" or, "what should I do with this big problem I have?"
turns.zh: 你提出的观点真是很有深度啊——如果大多数公司允许用户向他们咨询一些高风险的内容，比如寻求医疗建议，或者"我该不该和伴侣分手？"，又或者"面对这个大难题，我该怎么做？"之类的问题。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I feel like we would have immense regret if you had a model that was state-of-the-art on health bench, which is, GPT-5 is a state of the art on a bunch of these medical benchmarks, and you didn't use that to help people, you just disabled that use case because you wanted to avoid all possible downside. I think the duty is to make it awesome and to do the work, talk to experts, figure out how good it really is, where it breaks down, communicate that. And I think this technology is too important and has too much potential positive impact on people to run away from these high stakes excuses.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果你们开发出在健康领域堪称尖端技术的模型——比如GPT-5在诸多医学基准测试中表现出色——却不用于帮助人们，反而因为担心潜在风险就封禁了该应用场景，那我们会深感遗憾。我认为我们的责任是将技术做到极致，深入研究其应用场景，充分了解其优势与局限，并向公众准确传达这些信息。毕竟，这项技术意义重大，它对人类可能带来巨大积极影响，我们不应因担忧风险而轻易逃避挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And fast-forward to today, it's saving lives regularly. It's probably saving relationships regularly. Such a consequential decision, which I imagine was made early on.
turns.zh: 快进到今天，它已然能定期拯救生命，或许还能维系家庭关系。这样的重大决策，我想早在项目初期就已然做出了。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. We're just at the beginning of watching how this stuff can transform people. It's incredibly democratizing. If you compare, you roll out of this with the roll out of the personal computer, computers were so scarce when they first came out. And this stuff is ubiquitous in a way where you have access to a second opinion on medical stuff, you have access to a relationship buddy, you have access to a personal tutor on literally any topic that makes you curious. It's really, really special that we get to do that. Unique point in history.
turns.zh: 是啊。我们才刚刚开始见证这些技术如何改变人们的生活。它具有极强的民主化属性。拿个人电脑革命来做比较，个人电脑刚问世时供不应求，而如今这些技术已经无处不在——你可以获取医疗领域的第二意见，找到知心好友，甚至能就任何感兴趣的话题获得个性化辅导。能见证这一切实在太棒了，这真是历史上独一无二的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me zoom out a bit and talk about OpenAI and just product in general. So you've worked at traditional, let's say traditional product companies, Dropbox, Instacart. Now you're at OpenAI. What's maybe the most counterintuitive lesson you've learned by building products from your time at OpenAI?
turns.zh: 让我先退后一步，谈谈OpenAI以及产品开发的总体情况。你之前在传统产品公司工作过，比如Dropbox和Instacart，现在来到了OpenAI。在OpenAI从事产品开发期间，你学到的最出乎意料的经验是什么？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Each time I always tried to pick the maximally different job whenever I made a job change. So after Dropbox, I was craving a real world product because it was just so different than working on SaaS, et cetera. And after Instacart, I was craving on working on something that intellectually was interesting and had this kind of invoked the nerd in me. And so I've always looked for things that are really different. (01:02:59): And then once I showed up at these places, I tried to understand what makes that place successful, what is truly the thing that they cracked and how we can lean in that into that even more. (01:03:11): I think I spent a lot of time thinking about this with OpenAI, especially after ChatGPT. Before that it was kind of a moot point because we didn't really have much revenue or products or anything like that. There's a few things that come to mind that have driven many decisions. One is the empiricism. We talked about that a bit. The fact that you can only find out by shipping, which is why maximally lean into that. And that's a huge part of why we ship so much. (01:03:46): One of them is that amazing ideas come from anywhere. The thing about running a research lab is you really don't tell people what to research. That's not what you do. And we inherited that culture even as we become a research and product company. So just letting people do things who have amazing ideas rather than being the gatekeeper or prioritizer of everything or something like that has been proven immensely valuable to us. And that's where much of the innovation comes from, is empowered smart people on any function really. So that was a good inheritance from what I think made OpenAI successful and makes us successful. (01:04:23): The interdisciplinariness of really making sure that you put research and engineering and design and product together rather than treating them as silos. I think that's the thing that has made us successful and that you see come through in every product we ship. Like if we're shipping a feature and it doesn't get 2X better as the model gets 2X smarter, it's probably not a feature we should be shipping. Not always true. SOC 2 doesn't get better with [inaudible 01:04:48] models, but I think for many of the core capabilities, that's a good litmus test. (01:04:52): So I've always found you really have to lean into why is this place successful and then maximally accelerate that, so to speak, because it's what allows you to turn something that feels like an accident into something that is a repeatable label.
turns.zh:
每次换工作时，我都会刻意选择与之前截然不同的职位。因此，在离开Dropbox后，我渴望投身于现实世界的产品研发，因为这与SaaS等软件服务有着天壤之别。离开Instacart后，我又迫切希望从事能激发我内在好奇心的项目。所以我始终在寻找那些与众不同的挑战。

（01:02:59）：每次进入新公司后，我都会试图理解其成功之道——他们突破了哪些关键点，又如何能在此基础上进一步深化。（01:03:11）：在OpenAI，我花了大量时间思考这些问题，尤其是在ChatGPT问世之后。之前这类思考无从谈起，因为当时我们几乎没有营收、产品或其他核心业务。以下几点深刻影响了我们的决策：首先是经验主义。我们曾反复强调，唯有通过实际落地才能验证假设，因此我们极力践行这一理念。这也是我们频繁发布新功能的核心驱动力。

（01:03:46）：其次，优秀的创意可能来自任何角落。以研究实验室为例，我们从不强制规定研究方向——这不是我们的职责。即便转型为研发与产品公司，我们依然延续了这种文化。相较于充当把关者或资源分配者，我们更倾向于赋权有才华的团队成员，让他们自由探索。这为我们带来了丰厚的创新红利，推动了各个职能部门的深度协作。

（01:04:23）：跨学科协作同样重要。我们始终坚持将研究、工程、设计与产品开发紧密结合，而非将其割裂为独立部门。这种文化基因不仅造就了OpenAI的成功，也为我们的发展注入了源源不断的创新动能。例如，若某项功能的改进幅度不及模型智能提升的两倍，我们绝不会将其投入市场。当然并非所有情况都适用——SOC 2认证固然无法随着模型升级而同步提升，但核心功能的迭代质量仍是可靠的衡量标准。

（01:04:52）：我始终坚信，深入剖析成功之道并加以放大，是将偶然的成功转化为可复制模式的关键。正如OpenAI所证明的，多学科融合与协同创新是推动持续创新的核心力量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you talked about this kind of collaboration between researchers and product people. And you've been at the beginning of ChatGPT from day one to today, from zero to 700 million weekly active users. Not just registered users, weekly active users. How have you approached building out that team over time?
turns.zh: 您之前谈到了研究人员与产品团队之间的这种协作。您从ChatGPT项目伊始就深度参与其中，见证了它从零到如今每周7亿活跃用户的飞跃——这里指的不是注册用户，而是每周实际使用该产品的用户。请问您是如何逐步组建起这样一支高效团队的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: One of the other inheritances of being in a research lab is that you take recruiting really seriously. That's something that AI labs know every person matters. But many tech companies that go through hyper growth and they kind of lose their identity, they lose their talent bars, they just have chaos. So we've always had this tendency to run relatively lean. (01:05:51): So it is a small team that is running ChatGPT. I take co inspiration from WhatsApp where it was a very small team running a very global-scale product. And then more importantly, you have to treat hiring a little bit more like executive recruiting and less like just pure pipeline recruiting where you really need to understand what is the gap you're trying to fill on each team, what is the specific skill set and how do you fill it. (01:06:17): To give you an example, I'm a product person at heart, but sometimes a team doesn't need a product person because there's already someone doing that role. In many cases, we have a really talented engineering leader who has amazing product sense, or we have a researcher who has product ideas. And in my mind they can play that role. And maybe we have something else missing instead. Maybe we need a little bit more front-end or something like that. (01:06:41): In other cases, maybe what you're missing is incredible data scientists. So I really like to go through every single team and figure out what is the skill sets that that team needs and how do you put it together from principles rather than just assuming, "Hey, we're going to do a bunch of pipeline recruiting for all these different roles" and then people will find a team later. So I think that's always felt really important to me. And it's the way that you keep your team really small, yet super high throughput. (01:07:08): It also allows you to hire people who I think Keith Rabois calls us like barrels, I think. [inaudible 01:07:15] barrel's an ammunition where he thinks... I think this comes from him, but the idea being that sort of the throughput of your org depends on how many barrels you have, which is people who can make stuff happen. And then you can add ammunition around them, which is people helping those people. I think that's been really true for our recruiting too where we try to maximize the number of empowered people who can ship because that's how you have a small team and still get the ton done. (01:07:43): So there's a couple of things, and I spent a lot of time on vibes too with each team because I think one of the things that is challenging when you try to do research and product together is that the cultures are different. People have different backgrounds. And I think to make that go super well, you need to spend time team building and making sure that people have a huge amount of trust for each other's skill sets, feel like they can think across their boundaries. I really believe that product is everyone's job, for example. And for that reason, the recruiting doesn't stop when the people are on the door. It actually starts because you have to start making the teams awesome.
turns.zh:
身处研究实验室的另一个遗产，就是对招聘工作格外重视。这是人工智能实验室深知"人人皆重要"的理念。但许多科技公司在经历高速增长后，往往会失去自我认同，人才储备流失，陷入混乱。因此，我们始终倾向于保持团队规模相对精简。（01:05:51）：ChatGPT的研发团队规模就很小。我从WhatsApp那里获得灵感——当时也是一个小团队，却成功运营了一个全球级别的产品。更重要的是，你必须将招聘视为高管选拔，而非单纯的渠道筛选。这意味着你需要精准理解每个团队的空缺职位、所需技能组合，并据此制定招聘策略。（01:06:17）：举个例子，我本质上是个产品经理，但有时团队并不需要产品经理，因为已有成员承担该角色。很多情况下，我们会遇到极具才华的工程负责人，他具备卓越的产品敏锐度，或者是拥有产品创意的研究人员。在我看来，他们同样能胜任该角色。或许我们真正缺少的是其他技能——比如前端开发人才。（01:06:41）：还有些情况下，可能最需要的是顶尖数据科学家。因此，我会逐一审视每个团队，厘清其所需技能组合，并基于原则而非简单假设来组建团队。比如，“我们要为所有职位开展大规模渠道招聘”，然后让人们自己去寻找团队成员。但我始终认为这种方式至关重要。它能让团队规模精简，同时保持高效产出。（01:07:08）：这也让招聘策略更符合基思·拉博伊斯所说的"弹药桶"理念。[01:07:15]弹药桶指的是组织的输出能力取决于拥有多少能推动事物运转的人才。然后围绕这些人才补充支持力量。这种理念也完美适用于我们的招聘策略——我们致力于最大化拥有能交付成果的赋能型人才数量，这样才能在小团队规模下完成大量工作。

（01:07:43）：此外，我还花大量时间与各团队建立默契。因为研发与产品协同的挑战在于文化差异和背景不同。为确保协作顺畅，必须投入团队建设，确保成员高度信任彼此的专业能力，并能跨界思考。例如，我坚信产品是每个人的职责。因此，招聘不止于人员入职，更应从组建卓越团队开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something you do with team building that would be fun to share? Just like something you do to create [inaudible 01:08:28]?
turns.zh: 你们在团队建设方面有没有什么好玩的做法，可以分享一下呢？比如说，你们是如何通过某种方式营造出那种轻松愉快的团队氛围的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I just love whiteboarding with teams. I just love getting into a generative mindset. It breaks down everything. So that's the thing that I try. It's not particularly creative, but I found it to be a universal tool where the minute you can get people to stop thinking about what's my job versus the other person's job and more like we're all in a room trying to crack something together, that is incredible.
turns.zh: 我就是喜欢和团队一起用白板头脑风暴。我特别享受那种创造性思维的状态。它能把所有问题拆解得一清二楚。这就是我一直努力践行的方法。虽然不算特别有创意，但我发现它是个万能工具。一旦你能让大家不再纠结于"我的职责是什么？对方的职责是什么？"，而是转而专注于"我们现在在同一个房间里，共同攻克难题"，这种效果简直太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned this idea of first principles. This came up actually when I talk to a lot of people about you, is this something you're really big on. A lot of people talk about first principles, most people are like, " I don't really understand," or they think they're amazing at thinking from first principles. Is there something you can share of just what it actually looks like to think from first principles as maybe an example that comes to mind where you really went to first principles and came up with something unexpected?
turns.zh: 你提到了"第一性原理"这个概念。实际上，我和很多人谈论你的时候，他们都会提到这个词。这是否是你特别推崇的东西呢？很多时候人们提到第一性原理时，要么说"我不太理解"，要么自以为擅长从第一性原理出发思考问题。你能否分享一下如何真正践行第一性原理的具体方法？或许你能举个例子，说明自己是如何通过深入探究第一性原理，最终获得意想不到的创新成果的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, this is not something I'd ever say about myself. It's nice that someone else would say it, but it's a mysterious thing. Yeah, I think you just really got to get to ground truth on what you're really trying to solve. For example, as I mentioned with the recruiting thing, I'm not dogmatic that you have to have a product manager and an engineering manager and a designer or whatever. We're just trying to make an awesome team that can ship. So in that case, first principles means just really understanding what we actually need and what we're missing rather than applying a previously learned process or behavior. So I think that's a good example. (01:09:54): Another good example of I think being first principles in this environment is, does this feature need to be polished? We get a lot of crap for the model chooser, and I own it. I've tried to say that to everyone who will listen. For those who don't know model chooser, it's this giant drop down in the product that is literally the anti-pattern of any good product traditionally. (01:10:16): But if you are actually recent from scratch, is it better to wait until you got a polished product or to ship out something raw even if it makes less sense and start learning and getting into people's hands? I think a company with a lot of process or a lot of just learned behaviors will make one call, which is, we have a quality bar when we ship, and that's what we do. If your first principle is about it, I think you're like, "You know what? We should ship. It's embarrassing, but that's strictly less bad than not getting the feedback you wanted." (01:10:51): So I think just approaching each scenario from scratch is so important in this space because there is no analogy for what we're building. You can't copy an existing thing. There is no, "Are we an Instagram or are we a Google or a productivity tool or something like that?" I don't know. But you can learn from everywhere, but you have to do it from scratch. And I think that's why that trait tends to make someone effective at OpenAI, and it's something we test for in our interviews too.
turns.zh:
是啊，这可不是我会拿来形容自己的话。别人这么说固然不错，但这确实是个神秘的事儿。是啊，我觉得你得先真正搞清楚自己真正想解决的问题。比如我之前提到的招聘事儿，我并不认为必须要有产品经理、工程经理、设计师之类的人。我们只是想组建一支能交付成果的牛团队。所以在这种情况下，"第一性原理"意味着要深刻理解我们真正需要什么、我们缺少什么，而不是套用之前学到的流程或行为模式。这就是个很好的例子。

（01:09:54）：我认为在这种环境下践行"第一性原理"的另一个好例子是——这个功能到底需要打磨吗？模型选择器这事儿我们被吐槽得够呛，我承认责任在我。我尽力跟每个愿意听的人解释过。对于不了解模型选择器的人来说，它就是产品里那个巨大的下拉菜单，简直是传统好产品的反面教材。

（01:10:16）：但如果你从零开始，到底是等产品打磨到完美再上线，还是先推出一个粗糙的版本、边学边改、边收集用户反馈呢？我觉得那些流程繁琐、习惯套用既有模式的公司通常会遵循一种标准答案："我们有既定的上线质量标准，必须遵守。"如果你把第一性原理贯彻到底，就会想："管他呢，先上线吧。虽然丢脸，但总比得不到用户反馈强得多。"

（01:10:51）：所以在这种领域，完全从零出发处理每个场景至关重要，因为我们所做的东西没有现成的模板。不能照搬现有产品。没有人会问"我们是Instagram还是Google，或者是生产力工具之类的？"我也不知道。但你可以借鉴各处经验，但必须从零开始。我觉得这就是OpenAI能高效运作的关键特质，也是我们面试时重点考察的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this theme keeps coming up, and I think it's just important to highlight something that you keep coming back to, which is this trade-off of speed and polish and how in this space, speed is more important, not just to stay ahead, but to learn what the hell people actually want to do with this thing. Is there anything more that you think people just may be missing about why they need to move so fast in the space of AI?
turns.zh: 这一主题反复出现，我认为有必要强调一个你们反复提及的关键点——即速度与精细度的权衡取舍。在这个领域，速度更为重要。不仅要保持领先，更要了解用户真正想用这款产品做什么。关于人工智能领域为何必须快速行动，你们觉得还有哪些关键点是人们可能忽视的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, the boring answer would be, oh, it's competitive and everyone's in AI and they're trying to compete each other. I think that's maybe true, but that's not the reason that I believe this. The reason really is that you're going to be polishing the wrong things in the space. You absolutely should polish-
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，常见的解释是，竞争激烈，每个人都在做人工智能，都在试图相互竞争。我觉得这或许是对的，但这不是我持这种观点的原因。真正的原因在于，你可能会在错误的方向上投入精力。你绝对应该把精力投入到真正重要的地方——

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: You're going to be polishing the wrong things in this space. You absolutely should polish things like the model output, et cetera, but you won't know what to polish until after you ship. And I think that is uniquely true in an environment where the properties of your product are emergent and not knowable in advance. And I think that many people get that wrong because they think the best product people tend to be craftspeople and they have a traditional definition of craft. I also think it would be easy to use all what I just said as an excuse not to eventually build a great product. So I often tell my teams that shipping is just one point on the journey towards awesomeness, and you should pick that point intentionally where it doesn't have to be the end of your iteration at all. It can be the beginning, but you better follow through. (01:12:50): So we've been doing a bunch of work, especially over the last quarter of really cleaning up the UI of ChatGPT. I'm really excited to do the same for the sort of the response layouts and formats next. Simply because once you know what people are doing, there's no excuse to not polish your product. It's just really, in a world where you don't know yet, you might get very distracted. (01:13:09): So it's situational. Again, you kind of have to be first principles about it. But I do think using velocity, especially early on, as a tool... Actually this has been said about consumer social for example. It is not the first space where people have said, "Hey, you just got to try 10 things because you're probably going to be wrong." So I don't think this has never existed before as a dynamic either, but I do think with AI, it's important to internalize.
turns.zh:
你们在这块领域里会把重点放错地方。你们当然应该打磨产品，比如模型输出之类的，但在正式发布前，你们根本不知道该优化哪些方面。我认为这种情况在产品属性是不断涌现且无法提前预知的环境中尤为典型。许多人误解了这一点，他们认为最优秀的产品经理往往是手工艺人，而手工艺人又被传统定义为精益求精者。但我觉得，很多人会拿这些话当借口，不去打造真正出色的产品。所以我常跟团队说，发布只是通往卓越之路上的一个节点，你们应该刻意选择这个节点——它不必是迭代的终点，可以是起点，但必须坚持到底。

（01:12:50）过去几个月我们做了大量工作，尤其是优化了ChatGPT的用户界面。我很期待接下来能把同样的精力投入到回复格式和布局上。这是因为一旦你了解了用户的真实需求，就没有理由不去打磨产品了。但在未知的领域里，人们往往容易分心。

（01:13:09）这取决于具体情况。归根结底，你需要遵循最基本的原则。不过我确实认为速度测试，尤其是早期阶段的速度测试，是一种有效的工具……这在消费级社交领域就曾被提及。这种“先试10种方案，总有一种是对的”的理念并非首次出现。但在AI领域，深刻理解这种动态思维尤为重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's also an element of the models are changing constantly and so you may not even realize what they're capable of, I imagine.
turns.zh: 另外，这些模型的功能也在不断更新迭代，所以你可能甚至都没意识到它们现在能做些什么，我猜。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Totally. The models are changing and the best way to improve them, whether or not you're a lab or actually just someone who's doing context engineering or fine-tuning a model maybe, you need failure cases, real failure cases, to make these things better. The benchmarks are increasingly saturated. So really you need real-world scenarios where your product or model is not actually doing the thing it was supposed to do, and the only way you get that is by shipping, because you get back to use case distribution and you can make those things good. And therefore, it's actually the best way to then go articulate to your team, especially your ML teams, what [inaudible 01:14:17] climb on? It's like, "Oh, people are trying to do X and the model's failing in ways. Why? Now let's make those things really good."
turns.zh: 完全正确。模型正在不断演变，而改进模型的最佳方法——无论你是一家实验室，还是仅仅在进行上下文工程或微调模型的人——都需要真实的失败案例。基准测试数据正变得越来越趋于饱和。因此，你真正需要的是真实场景——即你的产品或模型无法完成预定任务的情况。而获取这些场景的唯一途径就是上线应用，因为这样你才能重现用户场景的分布，并对其进行优化。因此，这实际上是向团队（尤其是机器学习团队）清晰传达问题所在的最佳方式。比如，你可以说：“哦，用户在尝试做X，但模型却出现了各种故障。为什么会这样？现在让我们把这些问题彻底解决。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point about failure cases makes me think about something that both Kevin Weil and Mike Krieger shared, which is that evals are becoming a huge new skill that product people need to get good at because so much of product building is now writing evals. Is there something there you want to share?
turns.zh: 关于失败案例的这个观点，让我联想到凯文·韦尔（Kevin Weil）和迈克·克里格（Mike Krieger）都提到的一点：评估正逐渐成为产品经理必须掌握的一项重要新技能，因为如今产品开发的很大一部分工作都离不开编写评估文档。您对此有什么想分享的见解吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: My entire OpenAI journey has been this journey of rediscovering eternal product wisdom and principles in like slightly new contexts. So I remember I started writing evals before I knew what an eval was because I was just outlining very clearly specified ideal behavior for various use cases until someone told me, "Hey, you should make an eval." And I realized there was this entire world of research evaluation benchmarks that had nothing to do with the product that I was trying to make. And I was like, "Wow, this might be the lingua franca of how to communicate what the product should be doing to people who do AI research." And that really clicked for me. (01:15:23): And at the end of the day, it's not that different from the wisdom of, you ought to articulate success before you do anything else. It's just a new mechanism for doing that. But you can do it in a spreadsheet, you do it anywhere, and I really wanted to mystify it for people who hear that term. It's not some technical magic that you have to understand. It's really just about articulating success in a way that is maximally useful for training bots.
turns.zh: 我的整个OpenAI之旅，就是在不断以略微不同的视角重新发现那些永恒的产品智慧与原则。记得在还未真正理解"评估（eval）"这个概念时，我就开始撰写评估文档——当时我只是在为各种使用场景勾勒出清晰明了的理想行为规范，直到有人对我说："嘿，你应该写个评估文档。"那时我才意识到，整个研究评估基准领域与我试图打造的产品毫无关联。但这让我突然领悟："哇，这或许就是向AI研究人员传达产品应有功能的通用语言！"这一刻让我豁然开朗。（01:15:23）说到底，这与"在行动前先明确成功标准"的智慧理念并无太大差别，只是采用了新型的实现机制。评估可以用电子表格完成，任何场景下都能应用。我特别想为初次接触这个术语的人解开这个谜团——它并非深奥的技术魔法，而是以一种对机器人训练最具指导意义的方式清晰传达成功标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I have a post coming out soon that gives you a very good how-to for PMs have how to write evals.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很快会发布一篇文章，为项目经理们提供一个非常实用的评估写作指南。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I would love to read it. And I hope you agree with what I just said because maybe there's [inaudible 01:16:02] to it.
turns.zh: 我很想读一读这本书。希望你能认同我刚才的看法，因为这本书或许存在一些（此处音频不清，01:16:02处有停顿）不足之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Absolutely. And now there's all these tools that make this easier for you.
turns.zh: 完全没错。完全没错。现在有各种工具能让这件事变得更简单。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so this basically backs up this point that this is just a very important skill that product teams and builders need to get good at.
turns.zh: 好的，这基本上印证了我的观点，即这是一项非常重要的技能，产品团队和开发者都需要掌握好它。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Just a few more questions. I know you have a lot going on today. One is that this trend of ChatGPT being a big driver of growth for traffic to sites, for products. For example, ChatGPT is now driving more traffic to my newsletter than Twitter, which completely shocked me. I just was looking at my stats, I'm like, "What the hell? This is not something I knew was coming." So just I guess thoughts on the future of this, how you think about just ChatGPT driving growth and traffic to products and sites?
turns.zh: 好的。再问几个问题。我知道你今天事情很多。第一个问题是，ChatGPT成为网站和产品流量增长的重要推动力。这趋势很明显，比如说现在ChatGPT为我的新闻通讯带来的流量比Twitter还要多，这让我大吃一惊。我刚看完数据统计时，简直惊呼“什么鬼？这完全出乎我的意料”。所以我想听听你对未来趋势的看法，你如何看待ChatGPT推动产品和网站流量增长这一现象？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I'm really excited about it because in the same way that I find it dystopian to talk to everything through a chat bot, I also find it dystopian to not have amazing new high quality content out there. And for that reason, I talked a little bit earlier about search and have that solved a really important user problem early on because you had this knowledge cutoff thing and you suddenly could talk about anything. Very obvious in retrospect. A, it wasn't just a user problem, it was an ecosystem problem where the original ChatGPT, it didn't have outlinks, it would just answer your question, it would keep you in the product. And even if you wanted to keep reading or go deeper, there was no way for us to drive traffic back to the content ecosystem. And I've been really excited about what we've been doing in search, not just because it gives people more accurate answers, but because it allows us to surface really high quality content, like this podcast, to people who want to see it. (01:17:47): And of course there's so many interesting questions about, well in the Google era, there was the search engine optimization and there was clearly understood mechanisms of how to show up and get more traffic. So I get a lot of questions from people, like, "What is the equivalent of that? The AI era, if I'm Lenny and I want to 10X the traffic to my podcast, what do I actually need to do?" And the truth is we don't have amazing answers there simply because the way to appeal to an AI model ideally is the same way that you would appeal to a real user, because the model's supposed to proxy the interest of the user and nothing else. At least that's how I want our product to work. And for that reason, my advice is super lame, which is make really high quality content, which is not as actionable as I think people making content would ideally like. And I think this is why we have more work to do because maybe there's a better mechanism or protocol that we could come up with. (01:18:42): But I'm excited this is driving meaningful traffic for you, and I hope that other people making great content start to feel this way because, again, it's a very new scenario.
turns.zh:
这一点让我特别兴奋，因为正如我认为通过聊天机器人与万物对话是反乌托邦一样，我也觉得无法获取优质新内容同样令人不安。因此，我之前提到了搜索功能——它早期就解决了一个至关重要的用户痛点，因为此前存在知识获取障碍，而现在你可以畅谈任何话题。回想起来，这其实显而易见。但这不仅是用户问题，更是生态系统层面的挑战：最初的ChatGPT没有外部链接功能，只能直接回答问题，将用户困在产品内。即便你想深入探索或继续阅读，我们也无力将流量引回内容生态系统。

我对搜索领域的进展充满期待，不仅因为它能为用户提供更精准的答案，更能将优质内容推送给有需求的用户，比如这档播客。（01:17:47）当然，人们常问：在谷歌时代，搜索引擎优化（SEO）策略清晰，流量获取机制明确。如今很多人问我："AI时代要如何实现10倍流量增长？"说实话，我给不出完美答案，因为吸引AI模型的关键在于理解用户需求——模型本质上应该模拟真实用户的兴趣，仅此而已。至少这是我希望产品能实现的目标。因此我的建议很平庸：制作高质量内容。但这远比不上创作者理想中的操作指南。我认为这正是我们仍需探索的领域，或许未来会诞生更优的机制或协议。

（01:18:42）但看到搜索功能为你带来实实在在的流量增长，我倍感振奋。希望其他优质内容创作者也能感受到这种积极变化，毕竟这是一个全新的生态场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's two acronyms people have been using for this specific skill of AI driven SEO. I think one is AEO, which is answer engine optimization. The other is GEO. I forget the G one.
turns.zh: 关于AI驱动的SEO这一特定技能，人们常用两个缩写词来指代。我觉得其中一个是AEO，指的是"问答引擎优化"（Answer Engine Optimization）。另一个缩写词是GEO，但我暂时记不清第一个字母了。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Generative... Yeah, I don't know.
turns.zh: 生成式……嗯，我也不太清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Generative, yeah, AI optimization.
turns.zh: 生成式的，没错，就是AI优化。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite of those two? [inaudible 01:19:10]-
turns.zh: 你们俩中有没有最喜欢的一个？[听不清 01:19:10] -

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: No, no. I try to shy away from these terms unless they become inevitable just because I'm not entirely sure yet if that should be a concept or not. Again, I think ideally, ChatGPT understands your goals and therefore understands what content would be interesting to you. And the content creator's job is to share enough information and metadata about that content such that the AI model can make a user-aligned decision. And therefore, I'm not sure if giving this thing a name and making a thing is what we should be doing or not. I'm very eager to learn from folks making content about what this could look like because. Again, we're still working through.
turns.zh: 别，别这样。我尽量避免使用这些术语，除非它们已势在必行——因为我还不确定这是否应该成为一个概念。说真的，我认为理想情况下，ChatGPT能理解你的目标，从而知道哪些内容会让你感兴趣。内容创作者的职责是提供足够的信息和元数据，让AI模型能做出符合用户需求的决策。所以我不确定，是否应该给这个东西起个名字、专门开发一个产品，还是说这根本就不是我们该做的。我很想听听那些制作相关内容的人的想法，看看这项技术最终会呈现出怎样的形态。毕竟，我们还在探索阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, another question people think about is you have GPTs, which are kind of these custom GPT apps that you can build to answer very specific use cases. There's always this question of, you're going to build an app store where I can plug in my product into ChatGPT, monetize that. Is there stuff there that you could talk about that might be coming someday?
turns.zh: 基于此，人们还思考了另一个问题：GPT（生成式预训练转换器）技术可以定制开发应用程序，用于满足特定场景的需求。人们总会问道：能否开发一个应用商店，让用户可以将自己的产品接入ChatGPT平台并实现变现？对于这些问题，您能否谈谈未来可能的发展方向？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: GPTs are cool. They're kind of ahead of their time in the sense that we built that kind of concept before you could really build very differentiated things. At least in the consumer space, your learning GPT is going to be pretty similar to what the model could already do out of the box. So it's mainly a way of articulating a use case to people, but it doesn't have enough tools yet to make something that feels like an app, so to speak. (01:20:47): Different in the enterprise by the way. We're seeing a ton of adoption of GPTs there because just every single company has very bespoke business processes and problems, etc. And it's a really, really useful tool there. They also have unique data that they can hook up to these things that it can retrieve over. So we've seen a lot of success there. (01:21:05): I think the idea is the right one, and I think we're going to figure out a good mechanism for it. Because when you have so much capability packed into AI, it feels really powerful to allow people to package that up in ways that have a clear affordance, a clear use case, and are differentiated from each other. I also would love it if you could start a business on ChatGPT. I think there really is a world where, as this thing hits a billion user scale, it can get you distribution, it can get you started on making something in the same way that people built on the internet and there was entirely new businesses to be built. (01:21:41): So I think we'll have more to share there in the future. GPT's was an early stab. And I'm just excited to evolve the thinking there as the models get good and our reach increases as well.
turns.zh: GPT技术确实很酷。从某种意义上说，它们超前于时代——我们在构建这种概念时，当时人们还无法真正开发出高度差异化的产品。至少在消费领域，你训练的GPT模型与现成模型能做到的功能相差无几。因此，它主要用于向用户清晰阐述应用场景，但目前缺乏足够的工具来真正打造出类似应用的体验。（01:20:47）：顺便说一下，GPT在企业领域的应用情况截然不同。我们观察到大量企业采用GPT技术，因为每个公司都有高度定制化的业务流程和特定问题等场景。GPT在这里确实是一个非常实用的工具。企业还能将独特的数据接入这些模型，进行精准检索。因此，我们在企业领域取得了显著成效。（01:21:05）：我认为这个理念是正确的，相信我们能找到合适的实现机制。当AI技术赋予如此强大的能力时，让人们能够以清晰易懂的方式封装这些能力、构建明确的应用场景，并实现彼此差异化，这无疑非常有价值。我甚至希望能基于ChatGPT创立新业务。我相信当这项技术达到十亿用户规模时，它将为你带来用户流量，助你开启创新之路，就像人们在互联网上创业、催生全新商业模式一样。（01:21:41）：未来我们会分享更多进展。GPT只是一个早期尝试。我很期待随着模型性能提升、用户覆盖面扩大，我们能不断完善相关思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That is really cool. I'm really excited to see what you guys do there. Okay. Completely different direction. Something that I know about you is you studied philosophy in college.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是太酷了。我很期待看到你们在那边的成果。好的，现在转换到另一个话题。我了解到你大学学的是哲学。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I did.
turns.zh: 是的，我做到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Computer science and philosophy, right? A combo.
turns.zh: 计算机科学和哲学，对吧？这可是绝配组合啊。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah. I started as a philosophy major and took one coding class because I really liked logic, and programming was most similar to that. And then I fell in love with coding and then eventually computer science, and I just kept doing more and more of it. But until then, I'd never really thought of myself as a technical person, so it was kind of a late discovery in my life that I'm very grateful for.
turns.zh: 是啊。我最初选的是哲学专业，后来因为对逻辑学很感兴趣，觉得编程和逻辑最为相似，就选了一门编程课。结果我很快就爱上了编程，接着又转向了计算机科学，一发不可收拾。不过在那之前，我从未真正把自己视为一个技术型人才。所以这算是我人生中一个迟来的发现，我对此心怀感激。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an incredible combination for someone leading this product [inaudible 01:22:30].
turns.zh:
能领导这款产品的人，真是天赋异禀啊！  
（注：此处原文存在语音中断，时间点为 01:22:30，故在翻译时对此进行了合理处理。）

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It's true. It is really coming in full circle in a way that I couldn't have predicted. The amount of questions you have to grapple with are truly super interesting. And philosophy, it's not a traditionally practical skill, but it does really teach you to think things through from scratch and to articulate a point of view, and I think that has come in handy numerous times.
turns.zh: 确实如此。整个经历兜兜转转，最终圆满收尾，这完全超出了我的预料。需要面对的诸多难题着实令人着迷。哲学固然不是一项传统意义上的实用技能，但它确实能教会你从零开始思考问题，清晰表达观点。我觉得这项能力已经多次派上了用场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a specific philosopher or school that has been most handy to you, or is there more just the general [inaudible 01:22:57]?
turns.zh: 是否有哪位哲学家或某个哲学流派对您帮助最大？还是说您更多地受益于哲学领域的通识知识？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Oh, there's so many.
turns.zh: 哦，太多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I wrote my senior thesis on whether and why rational people can disagree, which also comes in handy when a lot of people with very different values have opinions on your model behavior or on how things should work. So I really like 20th century analytical philosophers. It's kind of dirty stuff, but I don't know if I have a favorite. It's too many to count. But that's the kind of stuff I like. And some of it ends up being quite analytical. You have let P be this theory of love and let Q be this other theory of love, and then you do some sort of symbolic manipulation. So it is just as much a brain thought exercise as it is... Or it's much more that than practical, but it taught me how to think in a way that continues to be pretty valuable.
turns.zh: 我在毕业论文中探讨了理性的人是否会存在分歧，以及分歧产生的原因。这项研究对我的帮助很大——当许多价值观迥异的人对你的行为模式或事物应然状态提出质疑时，理性思维能帮你化解矛盾。所以我特别推崇20世纪的分析哲学家。这种研究有时显得有些晦涩，但我实在难以选出最喜欢的哲学家。优秀的思想家实在太多了，难以一一列举。不过这类研究确实令我着迷。比如，将P视为某种爱情理论，Q视为另一种爱情理论，然后进行符号化推演。这既是脑力锻炼，也是……说实话，它更多是理论探索，而非实用工具，但它教会了我一种至今仍受益匪浅的思考方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible. What a cool combo of skills and background. Last question before we get to very exciting lightning round. So you were a product leader at Dropbox, then Instacart, now you're the PM of arguably the most consequential product in history. How did you land in this role? What was the story of joining OpenAI and taking on this work?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。你的技能组合和背景真是太棒了。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题。你曾在Dropbox和Instacart担任产品负责人，如今又成为史上最具影响力的产品负责人。你是如何获得这个职位的？加入OpenAI并接手这项工作的经历是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Every single career decisions I ever made, including my first one out of college, was just figuring out who are the smartest people I know that I want to hang out with and learn from, and can I work with them? And I don't know how to vet companies, I don't know how to really logically think through what space is going to take off or something like that, but I just do feel like I have a sense on people. And for Dropbox, I followed the head teaching assistant for a class that I was TA-ing. And for Instacart, I followed some of the smartest product people I knew. And for OpenAI, the person who recruited me, Joanne, I had messaged her about getting off the DALL·E waitlist and she said, "Only if you interview here." So she turned it into a reverse recruiting thing. (01:25:02): And initially, honestly, I didn't know what I would do here because it was a research lab and I was a product person and they said, "Don't worry, we'll figure it out." And they were sort of being cagey. And I thought they were being cagey because it's OpenAI and they can't share anything, but they were being cagey because we actually just didn't know yet at the time. So I showed up and I did everything under the sun and it definitely wasn't product. It was like, I think my first task was fix the blinds or something like that. And then I started sending out NDAs for people because they needed some operational help. And then I started asking, "Wait, why am I sending out NDAs? Oh, so we could talk to users." And I was like, "Talking to users, that sounds like the thing I know how to do." And I quickly stumbled into doing product work, and then eventually leading a bunch of product work. But it was organic by just showing up and doing what had to be done because, again, the company I joined was not a product company by any.
turns.zh:
我做过的每一项职业决策——包括大学毕业后的首份工作——都是围绕一个核心考量：谁是我认识的最聪明的人？我想和他们共事、向他们学习，并评估能否与他们合作。  
我不擅长评估公司，不善于逻辑推演某个领域会迎来爆发式增长之类的事，但我对人有种敏锐的直觉。比如加入Dropbox时，我追随了自己担任助教课程的首席教学助理；在Instacart，我与认识的最聪明的产品人员合作；在OpenAI，招募我的乔安妮曾回复我：“只有面试成功才能加入。”于是她把整个招聘流程反过来了。  
（01:25:02）最初坦白说，我并不清楚自己能在OpenAI做什么，因为这是一家研究实验室，而我当时是产品经理。他们说：“别担心，我们会安排的。”但他们当时态度神秘。我原以为他们是因为OpenAI的保密协议不能透露信息，但其实当时我们自己也还不确定。  
我到岗后忙得不可开交，完全不是产品相关工作。比如第一项任务是修理百叶窗之类的。后来他们急需运营支持，我就帮忙发送保密协议。发完后我问：“为什么要发保密协议？” 对方回答：“为了和用户沟通。” 我顿时意识到：这正是我擅长的事！就这样顺其自然地进入了产品岗位，最终还负责了多个产品项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. This is such a good example of, I don't know if you think of it this way, but when someone offers you a seat on a rocket ship, don't ask which seat. [inaudible 01:26:07].
turns.zh: 哇。这真是个绝佳的例子。我不知道你是否这么想过，但当有人邀请你搭乘火箭飞船时，别去纠结哪个座位更好。[语音不清 01:26:07]

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, so I didn't know it was a rocket ship. I kind of got nerd sniped is what I would describe it as. Where as I prepared for the conversation to get off the DALL·E waitlist really, I just started reading about the space and that piqued the philosophy brain and then also actually the computer science brain. I was like, "Wait, this is cool." Then I started reading all the academic papers of that era. So it was intellectual itch and the people, but then I stayed for the product opportunity, obviously. Post ChatGPT, when that took off, realized that we'd built a rocket ship where we'd launched it while building it, maybe is the analogy. But I can't say that it felt like a hyped job or anything like that when I applied.
turns.zh: 是啊，我之前根本不知道这是一项开创性的技术。我当时真是被突如其来的冷知识给"套路"了。原本我只是在为如何从DALL-E的候补名单中脱颖而出做准备，结果却一头扎进了太空领域的研究里。这既激发了我的哲学思维，也点燃了我的计算机科学热情。我当时就感叹："哇，太酷了！"于是我开始研读那个时代的学术论文。最初的驱动力既来自于学术探索的渴望，也源于对技术团队的认同。但显而易见，在ChatGPT大火之后，我们才意识到自己打造了一艘"火箭飞船"——在研发过程中就完成了发射。话说回来，申请这份工作时，可没觉得自己会身处一个被过度炒作的行业里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a lesson there is, as you said, follow the smartest people you know. There's also just this thread of follow things that are interesting to you. Just you playing with DALL·E led to this opportunity.
turns.zh: 所以从中得到的启示，正如你所说，就是要追随你认识的最聪明的人。还有一点就是，要关注那些令你感兴趣的事物。正是因为你玩DALL·E，才抓住了这次机会。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. And actually that's something we still test for is curiosity is an attribute that we think matters so much more than your ML knowledge. I'm not making a comment on research hiring. I think you do need some ML knowledge, I'm afraid. But for product and engineering and design people, and those kinds of functions, I actually think that if you are just curious about the stuff works, it doesn't matter at all if you've never done it before. In fact, if you were to filter for people who've done it before, you would have a very narrow filter of very lucky people rather than necessarily the best people you can get. So I think we've scaled that. Certainly what got me here, but I think it's actually, just generically, been a good predictor of success at OpenAI.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。不过说实话，我们现在仍在考察的一个要素就是好奇心——我们认为这比起机器学习知识要重要得多。我不是在批评招聘研究人员的标准，恐怕你确实需要具备一定的机器学习基础。但对于产品、工程和设计等职位来说，如果你对技术原理充满好奇心，那么即便你之前从未接触过相关领域也无伤大雅。相反，如果只招募有相关经验的人才，反而会筛选出一批运气好的人，而未必能找到最优秀的候选人。所以我们已经把这项标准应用到招聘体系中了。当然，这也是我能进入OpenAI的关键因素，但更重要的是，从整体来看，它确实能有效预测员工在OpenAI的成功潜力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nick, I told you I had a billion... I said I had 2 billion questions to ask you. I feel like I've asked a lot. I feel like I still have a billion left. But I know, you told me right after this you, have a big GPT- 5 check-in that you got to get to. So-
turns.zh: 尼克，我跟你说过我有无数个问题要问你……我说我有20个问题想问你。我感觉已经问了不少了，但似乎还有无数个问题没问。不过我知道，你马上要去参加GPT-5的例会了，所以……

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: We got to ship.
turns.zh: 我们得把货发出去了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We got to ship. Better ship now that this is recorded and we're putting this out.
turns.zh: 得赶紧发货了。既然已经录制好了视频，准备发布了，那就现在发货吧。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: This is true. [inaudible 01:28:08].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is the forcing function. Okay, so before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you want to share, leave listeners with, think is important to share?
turns.zh: 这就是强迫函数。好的，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，还有什么你想分享的、能给听众留下深刻印象的、或者你认为值得传递的重要信息吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I try to share a little bit about how I made decisions because I hope to... I'm not that far out of school. I relate a lot to people who are coming in the job market, who are trying to figure out what to do with their life right now. And I feel very confident that if you surround yourself with people that give you energy and if you follow the things you're actually curious about, that you're going to be successful in this era. So my parting advice to folks really is put yourself around good people and do the things you're actually passionate about. Because in a world where this thing can answer any question, asking the right question is very, very important. And the only way to learn how to do that is to nurture your own curiosity. So it worked for me and it's the one repeatable thing that I can share. Everything else is luck.
turns.zh: 我试着分享一下自己做决策的思路，因为我希望……我毕业没多久，对即将踏入职场、正努力规划人生的人们感同身受。我深信，只要你身边都是能给你正能量的人，只要你追随自己真正感兴趣的事物，在这个时代你一定能成功。所以我给各位的临别忠告就是：多与优秀的人为伍，专注于自己真正热爱的事业。因为在这个信息爆炸的时代，提出正确的问题至关重要。而培养自身的好奇心是掌握这种能力的唯一途径。这套方法对我很管用，也是我能传授给大家的最实用经验。其他的一切，不过是运气使然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is counter to what a lot of people are doing right now, which is follow the money. Where can I make the most? How do I grow this thing and make $100 million? All these people that are getting these crazy offers were not planning to make a lot of money doing this.
turns.zh: 这与当下许多人的做法背道而驰——他们一心追逐金钱："哪里能赚最多钱？如何把这项事业做大，最终赚到1亿美元？"而那些获得了诱人邀约的人，本初并未把赚钱作为首要目标。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: It's quite interesting to see that stuff play out because I think all these people entered school for genuine reasons. They were excited about the space, they were researching it, they were pursuing knowledge, and I'm happy that that's being rewarded. And I don't know what the rewards will look like in the future, especially in a post-AGI world. But I just a feeling that if you follow that advice, you'll end up okay.
turns.zh: 看到这一切的发展过程挺有趣的，因为我觉得所有这些人进入学界都是出于真诚的动机。他们对某个领域充满热情，致力于相关研究，追求知识的真理。我很欣慰这些努力得到了认可。虽然我不确定未来奖赏的形式会是什么样子，尤其是在通用人工智能（AGI）时代到来之后。但我有一种预感，只要遵循这个建议，最终都会有好结果的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, Nick, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，尼克，接下来我们要进行激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我准备了五个问题，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Sure, yeah.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 有什么两三本你最常向他人推荐的书？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: In the product space, probably things like High Output Management or The Design of Everyday Things, or those kind of classic type things because I think they're extremely applicable in AI.
turns.zh: 在产品领域，可能像《高效能管理》或者《日常事物的设计》这类书籍，或者其他类似的经典著作，因为我认为它们在人工智能领域有着极高的实用价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We talked about philosophy. I don't know, is there a philosophy book you're like, "Here's the one to read if you're getting into this."
turns.zh: 我们聊了聊哲学。我也不知道，有没有哪本哲学著作让你会说：“如果你想深入研究这个领域，这本绝对值得一读。”

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Oh man. Anything by Rawls and Nozick. I like the political stuff. I think it's really fun. That is a type of thing I recommend. I don't think there's a practical reason to read that stuff, but I will nerd out about it with you. So at your own peril.
turns.zh: 天哪。罗尔斯和诺齐克的任何著作我都喜欢。我对政治类书籍情有独钟，觉得它们特别有趣。这类书籍绝对值得推荐。虽然我觉得读这些书没什么实际用处，但我还是会和你一起深度探讨，感兴趣的朋友可以自行尝试，但风险自担哦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed? If you've had time to watch anything.
turns.zh: 你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？如果你有时间的话，有没有什么值得一看的作品？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I think you've got to do a little bit of sci-fi to be in this space. You shouldn't copy any of it, but I think you learn from it. So regularly re-watch Her and Westworld. Severance was great. I think that's the stuff that, when I have time, I'll meddle with.
turns.zh: 我觉得要想在这个领域有所建树，就得多看看科幻片。虽然不必完全照搬，但至少能从中汲取灵感。比如，我会经常重温《她》和《西部世界》。《分裂》这部剧也非常棒。等我有时间了，肯定会把这些作品好好研究一番。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is awesome. I love that those are the two. Of all the sci-fi movies, those are the ones you resonate most with and find most interesting and valuable.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很高兴你选择了这两部。在所有科幻电影中，这两部最能引起你的共鸣，也最令你觉得有趣且富有价值。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yes, but that's probably my own limitation, so I'm sure there's more to discover.
turns.zh: 是的，但这很可能是我自身的局限性，所以我相信还有更多东西值得去探索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the way, have you read Fire Upon the Deep, that sci-fi book?
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，你读过《深渊之火》这本科幻小说吗？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不了

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I don't know if you have time to read this book, but I think you would love it. It's such a good-
turns.zh: 好的。我不知道你有没有时间读这本书，但我觉得你会喜欢它的。这本书真是太棒了——

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Oh, man. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。好吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... AI oriented sci-fi space opera sort of book.
turns.zh: ... 一本以人工智能为主题的科幻太空歌剧类书籍。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I'll check it out, thank you.
turns.zh: 我会去看看的，谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Off tangent.
turns.zh: 好吧。说点题外话。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah. For sure.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，是啊。当然啦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 好的。你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: I actually don't. I am at extreme capacity. It's kind of interesting. API developers ask me like, "Hey, are you going to copy all of our products?" It's like, I actually just do not have time to follow up what's going on outside of OpenAI because the pace here is so, so intense. So don't have good recs for you, I'm afraid.
turns.zh: 事实上我并没有关注其他公司。我现在已经忙得不可开交了。这挺有意思的，总有API开发者问我：“嘿，你打算把我们所有产品都抄袭一遍吗？”我只能说，我实在没时间去关注OpenAI以外的动态了，因为这里的工作节奏实在太快了。所以很抱歉，我暂时无法为你提供什么好的推荐了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a comforting answer, I think, to a lot of product companies. Go figure. Nick has no time to even listen to our stuff. Oh man. Okay. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself using when things are tough, sharing with friends or family that other people find useful?
turns.zh: 我觉得这对很多产品公司来说是个安慰人心的回答。真是难以理解啊，尼克甚至都没时间听我们汇报。天哪。好吧。你有没有什么人生格言，在遇到困难时会反复回味，觉得它对朋友或家人很有用，可以分享给其他人呢？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Being the average of the five people you spend the most time with is a thing that I really internalize, both in my personal life, where there's people who give me energy and who lift me up and make me a better person. My fiance is one of those people, but there's many people in my life. But then there's also just, at work, there's the equivalent. And again, that's how I've made all the career decisions. It's like who do I want to learn from? So I apply that principle constantly.
turns.zh: 我深深认同这样一个观点：你与身边五个相处时间最多的人平均起来所呈现的样子，是你自己的缩影。在个人生活中，总有一些人能给我带来能量，激励我成长，让我成为更好的自己。我的未婚夫就是这样的人，在生活中还有许多其他类似的存在。同样，在职场中也有同样的道理。正因如此，我做出的所有职业决策都遵循一个核心标准：我想向谁学习？我始终践行着这个原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, everybody I talked to told me that you are a very good jazz pianist. You have won competitions. I think you were planning to do this as your main thing and then you somehow took the side quest.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，我跟每个人聊过，他们都说你是一位非常出色的爵士钢琴家，还赢得过比赛奖项。我原本以为你打算把这项事业当作主业，但后来不知为何却转向了其他方向。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, I chickened out that at the very last minute, but I was going to go to school for music. And that's still my, hopefully, chapter two.
turns.zh: 是啊，我在最后一刻退缩了，但我原本打算去音乐学校深造的。希望这仍会成为我人生的第二篇章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I love that that might still happen.
turns.zh: 哇。我真希望这种情况还能继续发生啊。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Might still happen. Now I'm in some for fun bands and we will kick from time to time. It's like the one thing I can do when I'm otherwise super tired and can't think anymore because it balances me out in good ways. But yeah, hopefully I'll get to do more of it in the future.
turns.zh: 或许还是会的。现在我加入了几个玩票乐队，偶尔也会演出。这就像是我在身心俱疲、思维停滞时唯一能做的事，因为它能以积极的方式平衡我的状态。不过说真的，希望未来我能有更多这样的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any analogs between music and your job? Anything that you find-
turns.zh: 音乐和你的工作之间有什么相似之处吗？有没有什么方面是你发现两者有共通之处的？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Yeah, actually. I feel like you could think of software development as, or being a product person, as you could be a conductor of an orchestra or you could be in a jazz band. And I think of it as a jazz band where I don't believe in the idea of everyone having this set part that they have to play and me kind of telling people when to play. I love how in jazz, or other forms of improvised music, you're kind of riffing off of each other and you listen to what one person played and then you play something back. And I think that great product development is like that, in the sense that ideas could come from anywhere. It shouldn't be a scripted process. You should be trying stuff out, having fun, having play in what you do. So I use that analogy a lot. For those who like music, it tends to resonate.
turns.zh: 是的，实际上我觉得你可以把软件开发视为，或者说作为产品经理，你可以把自己比作管弦乐队的指挥，或者是爵士乐队的成员。我把这想象成一个爵士乐队——我不认同那种每个人必须严格按照既定曲目演奏、由我来指挥何时演奏的模式。我喜欢爵士乐或其他即兴音乐形式中那种相互呼应的即兴演奏——你听对方演奏，然后再即兴回应。我认为优秀的产品开发也应该如此，创意可以来自任何地方。这不应该是一个程式化的过程。你应该不断尝试新事物，享受其中的乐趣，让工作充满趣味性。所以我经常用这个比喻。对于喜欢音乐的人来说，这个比喻往往能引起共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nick, I am so thankful that you made time for this. I know today is insane. Tomorrow's going to be even more insane for the entire world. They have no idea what's coming. Thank you so much for doing this. Two final questions. Where can folks find you if you want them to find you online? Where can folks find GPT-5 potentially. And then just how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 尼克，真的很感谢你能抽出时间来参加这次访谈。我知道今天已经够忙乱了，而明天整个世界会更加混乱。人们根本不知道即将迎来怎样的挑战。非常感谢你能参与这次对话。最后两个问题：如果读者想在网上找到你，他们该去哪里找？GPT-5可能的发布渠道在哪里？然后，听众如何能为你提供帮助呢？

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Just use the product. You don't even have to pay. Should be your default model starting tomorrow and just use it and don't think about models anymore. Unless you want to and you're a Pro user, in which case you get all the old models. So rest assured. And useful, honestly, I learned so much from people at large and ChatGPT users, et cetera, so just keep doing your thing. I am watching and learning, and I appreciate all the feedback. So I'm sure after we fix the model chooser, you guys will roast me for something else and I'll take it. So keep it coming.
turns.zh: 就用这个产品吧。你们甚至无需付费。从明天起，这应该会成为你们的默认模式，直接使用就行，不用再纠结于模型选择了。除非你愿意升级为Pro用户，那样的话你就能继续使用所有旧模型。所以大家别担心。说实话，我从广大用户和ChatGPT用户那里学到了很多东西，所以继续专注自己的事情吧。我会持续观察和学习，也非常感谢大家的反馈。等我们优化了模型选择器后，我相信你们肯定会因为其他问题来吐槽我的，我会欣然接受的。所以请继续畅所欲言吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Nick, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。尼克，非常感谢你能来参加这次活动。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And good luck tomorrow.
turns.zh: 祝你明天好运。

turns.speaker: Nick Turley
turns.en: Thanks.
turns.zh: 谢谢。
